seqz is worth a second look. “is rs equal to zero” is computed as “is rs, read as unsigned, less than 1”. The only unsigned value below 1 is 0. Tricks like this are why RISC-V needs so few real instructions.

32-bit operations on a 64-bit machine

C’s int is 32 bits. RV64 has a w version of most arithmetic: addw, subw, addiw, sllw, mulw, divw. They compute using the low 32 bits only, then sign-extend the 32-bit result into all 64 bits. When you see addw in compiler output, the source code was doing int math.

A first example

Compute (a + b) * (a - b) where a is in a0 and b is in a1, leaving the result in a0:

add  t0, a0, a1      # t0 = a + b
sub  t1, a0, a1      # t1 = a - b
mul  a0, t0, t1      # a0 = (a + b) * (a - b)

Read it the way the CPU does: three instructions, three registers written, in order. Nothing else happens.

Exercises

  1. Write instructions that compute a0 = 3 * a0 + 7 without using mul. (Hint: 3x = x + 2x, and 2x is a shift.)
  2. a0 holds a value. Write one instruction that sets a0 to 1 if it is negative and 0 otherwise. (There are two good answers: one uses a compare, one uses a shift.)
  3. What does li t0, 2048 turn into? Why can’t it be one addi?
  4. What is in t0 after addi t0, zero, -1 followed by srli t0, t0, 60?

title: Memory: loads and stores
html:
Registers hold a few values. Everything else lives in memory. RISC-V moves data between the two with exactly two kinds of instruction: loads copy bytes from memory into a register, stores copy bytes from a register into memory.

The instructions

ld   t0, 8(a0)       # t0 = the 8 bytes at address (a0 + 8)
sd   t0, 8(a0)       # write the 8 bytes of t0 to address (a0 + 8)

The form offset(register) means “the address is the value in the register plus the offset”. The offset is a 12-bit signed immediate, so -2048 to 2047. There is no other addressing mode. Any address calculation more complicated than register + constant must be done with separate arithmetic instructions first.

For each size there is a load and a store. Smaller loads come in signed and unsigned versions because the upper bits of the register must be filled (chapter 1):

SizeLoad (sign-extend)Load (zero-extend)Store
1 byte
2 bytes
4 bytes
8 bytes(Not needed)
lb
                              lbu
                                                              sb

lh
                              lhu
                                                              sh

lw
                              lwu
                                                              sw

ld
                                                              sd

Stores do not need two versions. A store of 1 byte just writes the low 8 bits of the register and ignores the rest.

Arrays

An array is a run of same-sized elements stored back to back. If the array starts at address base and each element is size bytes, element i is at:

address of a[i] = base + i * size

For an array of long (8 bytes each) starting at address 1000:

So a[2] is at 1000 + 2 × 8 = 1016. In assembly, the multiply by 8 is a shift left by 3. Here is a complete function that sums an array. It was run in an emulator against random inputs:

sum.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long sum(long *a, long n)
  # a0 = address of a[0], a1 = n
      .globl sum
  sum:
      li   t0, 0
                          # t0 = s = 0
      li   t1, 0
                          # t1 = i = 0
  loop:
      bge  t1, a1, done   # if i >= n, leave the loop
      slli t2, t1, 3
                          # t2 = i * 8   (each long is 8 bytes)
      add  t2, a0, t2     # t2 = address of a[i]
      ld   t3, 0(t2)
                          # t3 = a[i]
      add  t0, t0, t3     # s = s + a[i]
      addi t1, t1, 1
                          # i = i + 1
      j    loop
  done:
      mv   a0, t0         # the return value goes in a0
      ret

The .globl sum line tells the assembler to make the label sum visible to other files, so C code can call it. Chapter 7 covers these directives.

Read the loop body slowly. The C expression a[i] became three instructions: slli to turn the index into a byte offset, add to make the address, ld to fetch. Indexing is not free. There is arithmetic hidden in every [i].

Walking a pointer instead

The multiply-and-add for every element can be avoided. Keep a pointer p that starts at a and moves forward 8 bytes each step, and stop when it reaches the end address:

sum_ptr.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long sum_ptr(long *a, long n): walk a pointer instead of an index
      .globl sum_ptr
  sum_ptr:
      li   t0, 0
                          # s = 0
      slli a1, a1, 3
                          # a1 = n * 8 = size of the array in bytes
      add  a1, a0, a1     # a1 = end = address just past the last element
  1:
      beq  a0, a1, 2f     # if p == end, done
      ld   t1, 0(a0)
                          # t1 = *p
      add  t0, t0, t1     # s += *p
      addi a0, a0, 8
                          # p = p + 1 element (8 bytes)
      j    1b
  2:
      mv   a0, t0
      ret

The loop body went from 7 instructions to 5, and the index variable disappeared. This is not a trick humans invented for speed. It is exactly what compilers do, as chapter 8 will show with real compiler output. The labels 1:, 1b and 2f are local labels: 1b means “the nearest label 1 going backwards” and 2f means “the nearest label 2 going forwards”. They save you from inventing names like loop2_end.

Bytes and strings

A C string is an array of 1-byte characters ending with a zero byte. Finding its length means loading one byte at a time until the zero appears. Note lbu (one byte, unsigned) and addi 1 (one byte forward, not 8):

strlen.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long my_strlen(char *s): count bytes until the zero byte
      .globl my_strlen
  my_strlen:
      mv   t0, a0         # t0 = p = s
  1:
      lbu  t1, 0(t0)
                          # load ONE byte, zero-extended to 64 bits
      beqz t1, 2f         # zero byte marks the end of a c string
      addi t0, t0, 1
                          # p = p + 1 (one byte, not 8)
      j    1b
  2:
      sub  a0, t0, a0     # length = p - s
      ret

The length is the end pointer minus the start pointer. Pointer subtraction gives a byte count, and here each element is one byte, so it is also the element count.

Structs

A struct is a block of memory where each field sits at a fixed offset from the start. The compiler decides the offsets. The program only ever sees load from (pointer + offset).

point.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # struct point { long x; long y; };      x at offset 0, y at offset 8
  # long dist2(struct point *p, struct point *q)
  #   returns (p->x - q->x)^2 + (p->y - q->y)^2
      .globl dist2
  dist2:
      ld   t0, 0(a0)
                          # p->x
      ld   t1, 0(a1)
                          # q->x
      sub  t0, t0, t1     # dx
      mul  t0, t0, t0     # dx * dx
      ld   t1, 8(a0)
                          # p->y   (offset 8)
      ld   t2, 8(a1)
                          # q->y
      sub  t1, t1, t2     # dy
      mul  t1, t1, t1     # dy * dy
      add  a0, t0, t1
      ret

p->x is ld t0, 0(a0) and p->y is ld t1, 8(a0). Field names do not exist in the machine. Only offsets do.

Alignment and padding

A value of size n is naturally aligned if its address is a multiple of n. An 8-byte long should sit at an address divisible by 8. Some CPUs trap on unaligned access, others handle it slowly. The C compiler adds padding bytes inside structs to keep every field aligned:

struct s {
    char c;
                // offset 0, 1 byte
                // 7 bytes of padding
    long x;
                // offset 8 (must be a multiple of 8)
};
                // total size 16, not 9

Reorder fields from largest to smallest and padding usually disappears. This matters on GPUs too: chapter 14 shows a 16-byte load that only works because the data is 16-byte aligned.

Addresses of global data

For data stored at a fixed label in the program, la t0, label (load address) puts the label’s address into a register. It is a pseudo-instruction that becomes auipc (add a 20-bit constant shifted up to pc) plus addi. You will see it in chapter 7.

Exercises

  1. Write long max(long *a, long n) for n >= 1. Start with best = a[0] and loop from i = 1.
  2. Write void rev(long *a, long n) that reverses an array in place. Use two pointers, one at each end, that move toward each other. Careful with n = 0.
  3. Write long dot(long *a, long *b, long n), the dot product of two arrays.
  4. struct node { long val; struct node *next; }. Write long list_sum(struct node *p) that adds up a linked list ending in a null pointer. What are the offsets of val and next?
  5. In sum_ptr, what would go wrong if you replaced beq a0, a1 with blt a0, a1 and swapped the targets? When would it matter?

title: Control flow
html:
The CPU runs instructions in order, one after another, until an instruction changes pc. Every if, else, while, for, break and switch in every language becomes some combination of the instructions in this chapter.

Branches

A branch compares two registers and, if the condition is true, sets pc to a target label. If the condition is false, execution continues with the next instruction.

beq  rs1, rs2, label   # if rs1 == rs2, go to label
bne  rs1, rs2, label   # if rs1 != rs2
blt  rs1, rs2, label   # if rs1 <  rs2   (signed)
bge  rs1, rs2, label   # if rs1 >= rs2   (signed)
bltu rs1, rs2, label   # if rs1 <  rs2   (unsigned)
bgeu rs1, rs2, label   # if rs1 >= rs2   (unsigned)

Those six are the only real branch instructions. Everything else is a pseudo-instruction that swaps the operands or uses zero:

You writeReal instruction
bgt a, b, L
                                      blt b, a, L

ble a, b, L
                                      bge b, a, L

beqz a, L
                                      beq a, zero, L

bnez a, L
                                      bne a, zero, L

blez a, L
                                      bge zero, a, L

bgtz a, L
                                      blt zero, a, L

A jump with no condition is j label. The target of a branch is stored in the instruction as a distance from the current pc, not as a full address. That is why code can be loaded at any address and still work.

If and else

The pattern for an if-statement is: test the opposite condition, and jump over the code that should not run.

if (x < lo)
             return lo;
else if (x > hi) return hi;
else return x;
clamp.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long clamp(long x, long lo, long hi)
  #   if (x < lo) return lo; else if (x > hi) return hi; else return x;
      .globl clamp
  clamp:
      bge  a0, a1, 1f     # if x >= lo, go check the upper side
      mv   a0, a1         # x < lo: return lo
      ret
  1:
      bge  a2, a0, 2f     # if hi >= x, x is in range
      mv   a0, a2         # x > hi: return hi
  2:
      ret

“if x < lo” became “if x >= lo, skip ahead”. You will see this inversion in nearly every compiled if-statement. Read compiled branches as “the condition under which we skip”.

Loops

A while loop is a test at the top and a jump back at the bottom. Here is the max function from the last chapter’s exercise. Notice the inner if (skip the update when best is already bigger) sitting inside the loop:

max.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long max(long *a, long n)   assumes n >= 1
      .globl max
  max:
      ld   t0, 0(a0)
                          # best = a[0]
      li   t1, 1
                          # i = 1
  1:
      bge  t1, a1, 3f     # i >= n ? done
      slli t2, t1, 3
      add  t2, a0, t2
      ld   t3, 0(t2)
                          # t3 = a[i]
      bge  t0, t3, 2f     # if best >= a[i], skip the update
      mv   t0, t3         # best = a[i]
  2:
      addi t1, t1, 1
      j    1b
  3:
      mv   a0, t0
      ret

This loop has two branch instructions per iteration that are always executed: the test at the top and the j at the bottom. Compilers usually rewrite loops so the test is at the bottom. Then one branch per iteration does both jobs: it tests and jumps back. This is called loop rotation. The cost is one extra test before the loop starts, to handle the case where the loop runs zero times. You will see exactly this shape in compiler output in chapter 8:

    if (n <= 0) skip the whole loop      # test once, before the loop
loop:
    body
    if (not done) go to loop            # one branch per iteration

Reversing an array: two pointers

The reversal exercise from chapter 4 uses two pointers walking toward each other. The comparison is bgeu because addresses are unsigned numbers:

rev.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # void rev(long *a, long n): reverse in place with two pointers
      .globl rev
  rev:
      beqz a1, 2f         # empty array: nothing to do
      slli t0, a1, 3
      add  t0, a0, t0
      addi t0, t0, -8
                          # t0 = hi = address of the last element
                          # a0 = lo = address of the first element
  1:
      bgeu a0, t0, 2f     # stop when lo >= hi (addresses are unsigned)
      ld   t1, 0(a0)
                          # t1 = *lo
      ld   t2, 0(t0)
                          # t2 = *hi
      sd   t2, 0(a0)
                          # *lo = old *hi
      sd   t1, 0(t0)
                          # *hi = old *lo
      addi a0, a0, 8
                          # lo moves right
      addi t0, t0, -8
                          # hi moves left
      j    1b
  2:
      ret

Branchless code

A branch that the CPU cannot predict is expensive, about 15 to 20 cycles each time it guesses wrong (chapter 11 explains why). Sometimes you can compute the same result with arithmetic and no branch at all. Counting how many elements equal x, the obvious way:

ex_count.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long count_eq(long *a, long n, long x): how many elements equal x
      .globl count_eq
  count_eq:
      li   t0, 0
      slli a1, a1, 3
      add  a1, a0, a1
  1:
      beq  a0, a1, 3f
      ld   t1, 0(a0)
      bne  t1, a2, 2f
      addi t0, t0, 1
  2:
      addi a0, a0, 8
      j    1b
  3:
      mv   a0, t0
      ret

The branchless way: xor gives 0 exactly when the two values are equal, seqz turns that into 1 or 0, and you add it unconditionally:

ex_count_branchless.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # same as count_eq, but no branch inside the loop body
      .globl count_eq2
  count_eq2:
      li   t0, 0
      slli a1, a1, 3
      add  a1, a0, a1
  1:
      beq  a0, a1, 2f
      ld   t1, 0(a0)
      xor  t1, t1, a2     # t1 = 0 exactly when a[i] == x
      seqz t1, t1         # t1 = (t1 == 0) ? 1 : 0
      add  t0, t0, t1
      addi a0, a0, 8
      j    1b
  2:
      mv   a0, t0
      ret

The loop still has its loop branch, which is easy to predict (it goes the same way every time except the last). The data-dependent branch is gone. Both versions were tested against the same inputs and give identical results.

Branchless is not always faster. If the branch is predictable (for example the data is mostly one value), the branchy version is fine and does less work. Chapter 11 measures the real costs.

Switch statements and jump tables

A switch on a small dense range of values often compiles into a jump table: an array of addresses in memory. The code checks the value is in range, loads table[value], and jumps to that address with jalr (jump to the address in a register). One load and one indirect jump replace a long chain of comparisons. When you see a load followed by jr or jalr to a register, think “switch statement” or “function pointer”.

Exercises

  1. Write long gcd(long a, long b) using euclid’s algorithm: while b is not 0, set (a, b) to (b, a % b).
  2. Write long bsearch(long *a, long n, long x): binary search in a sorted array, returning the index of x or -1. Use a half-open range [lo, hi).
  3. Write void bubble(long *a, long n) that sorts an array with bubble sort.
  4. Rewrite the max loop with loop rotation: one branch at the bottom of the loop that both tests and jumps back.
  5. In clamp, the test is bge a0, a1. What goes wrong if you used bgeu and x was -5 with lo = 0?

title: Functions and the stack
html:
A function call needs three things: jump to the function, pass it arguments, and come back to the right place afterwards with a result. The hardware gives you one instruction for the jump-and-remember part. Everything else is a set of rules that every compiler agrees to follow, called the calling convention or ABI (application binary interface). If you follow the same rules, your assembly can call C and C can call your assembly.

Call and return

jal  ra, label      # ra = pc + 4 (the next instruction), then jump to label
jalr zero, 0(ra)    # jump to the address in ra, discard the "return address"

jal is “jump and link”. It saves the address of the instruction after itself into ra, then jumps. The function runs and finishes with ret, which is the pseudo-instruction for jalr zero, 0(ra): jump to whatever address is in ra. So pc returns to the instruction right after the call. You will usually write call label, a pseudo-instruction that the assembler and linker turn into jal or a two-instruction form that can reach further.

The problem with nested calls

There is only one ra. If function f calls function g, the call g overwrites ra with an address inside f. F’s own return address, the one that leads back to f’s caller, is destroyed. When f tries to ret, it jumps to the wrong place.

The same problem applies to any register f wants to keep: g is free to overwrite it. The solution is to save values in memory before the call and load them back after. The memory used for this is the stack.

The stack

The stack is a region of memory. The register sp holds the address of its top. The stack grows downward: to get space, you subtract from sp. To give space back, you add.

addi sp, sp, -16    # reserve 16 bytes: sp now points at them
sd   ra, 8(sp)      # store ra into the upper 8 bytes
...
ld   ra, 8(sp)      # load it back
addi sp, sp, 16     # release the 16 bytes

The RISC-V ABI requires sp to always be a multiple of 16. So frames are rounded up: a function that needs 3 slots of 8 bytes reserves 32 bytes, not 24.

The stack is just memory. Nothing stops you from corrupting it, and a function that forgets to restore sp, or stores past its reserved area, breaks every function above it.

The rules of the ABI

RegisterRoleWho must preserve it
a0.. a7Arguments 1 to 8; a0 (andCaller (the callee may
a1) return the resultoverwrite them)
t0.. t6TemporariesCaller
Return addressCaller
s0.. s11Saved registersCallee: if you use one, restore
it before returning
Stack pointerCallee: must be back to its
original value on return
ra
sp

“caller-saved” means: if you are the caller and you need the value after the call, you must save it yourself, because the callee may destroy it. “callee-saved” means: the callee promises the value is unchanged when it returns. If the callee wants to use an s register, it saves the old value first and restores it at the end.

This split is a trade-off. A leaf function (one that calls nothing) can use all the t and a registers freely and needs no stack at all. A function that makes calls puts values it needs across those calls into s registers, and pays to save and restore those s registers once, at entry and exit, instead of around every call.

A leaf function

square:
    mul  a0, a0, a0
    ret

No stack, no saving. Argument in a0, result in a0. Most small functions look like this after the compiler is done with them.

A recursive function

Factorial: fact(n) = n <= 1 ? 1 : n * fact(n - 1). This function calls itself, so it must save ra. It also needs n after the recursive call returns, so it keeps n in s0, which means it must save the caller’s s0 first.

fact.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long fact(long n): recursive.  fact(n) = n <= 1 ? 1 : n * fact(n - 1)
      .globl fact
  fact:
      li   t0, 1
      bgt  a0, t0, 1f     # n > 1: recursive case
      li   a0, 1
                          # base case: return 1
      ret
  1:
      addi sp, sp, -16
                          # make room for 2 slots on the stack
      sd   ra, 8(sp)
                          # save our return address (the call below overwrites ra)
      sd   s0, 0(sp)
                          # save s0 because we are about to use it
      mv   s0, a0         # s0 = n   (s registers survive calls)
      addi a0, a0, -1
                          # argument = n - 1
      call fact           # a0 = fact(n - 1)
      mul  a0, s0, a0     # a0 = n * fact(n - 1)
      ld   s0, 0(sp)
                          # restore s0 for our caller
      ld   ra, 8(sp)
                          # restore our return address
      addi sp, sp, 16
                          # give the stack space back
      ret

The first part of the function that reserves stack space and saves registers is called the prologue. The matching part at the end is the epilogue. Every non-leaf function you read will have them.

Here is the stack while fact(3) is running deepest, inside fact(1). Each call to fact made its own 16-byte frame. Addresses decrease going down:

When fact(2) stored its s0, the value it saved was 3: fact(3)’s n, which fact(3) had put in s0. So each frame holds the previous level’s n. On the way back, each level multiplies by its own n (in s0), then restores the previous level’s s0, and returns through its saved ra. The emulator checked this function for n from 0 to 14.

Two calls: fibonacci

fib(n) = n < 2 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2). Now there are two recursive calls, and the result of the first must survive the second. That needs a second saved register:

fib.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long fib(long n): fib(n) = n < 2 ? n : fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
      .globl fib
  fib:
      li   t0, 2
      blt  a0, t0, 1f     # n < 2: return n (already in a0)
      addi sp, sp, -32
                          # 3 slots used, keep sp a multiple of 16
      sd   ra, 24(sp)
      sd   s0, 16(sp)
      sd   s1, 8(sp)
      mv   s0, a0         # s0 = n
      addi a0, s0, -1
      call fib            # a0 = fib(n - 1)
      mv   s1, a0         # s1 = fib(n - 1), must survive the next call
      addi a0, s0, -2
      call fib            # a0 = fib(n - 2)
      add  a0, s1, a0     # result = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
      ld   s1, 8(sp)
      ld   s0, 16(sp)
      ld   ra, 24(sp)
      addi sp, sp, 32
  1:
      ret

Three 8-byte slots are needed (ra, s0, s1), which is 24 bytes, rounded up to 32 to keep sp a multiple of 16.

A loop that calls a function

This is the most common real pattern: a loop whose body calls something. Every value the loop needs across the call (the pointer, the end address, the running total) goes into an s register, because the call is allowed to destroy all t and a registers:

sumsq.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long square(long x)                 a leaf function: calls nothing
  # long sum_squares(long *a, long n)   calls square() in a loop
      .globl square
  square:
      mul  a0, a0, a0
      ret

      .globl sum_squares
  sum_squares:
      addi sp, sp, -32
      sd   ra, 24(sp)
      sd   s0, 16(sp)
                          # s0 = p
      sd   s1, 8(sp)
                          # s1 = end
      sd   s2, 0(sp)
                          # s2 = total
      mv   s0, a0
      slli a1, a1, 3
      add  s1, a0, a1
      li   s2, 0
  1:
      beq  s0, s1, 2f
      ld   a0, 0(s0)
                          # argument for square = *p
      call square         # may destroy every a and t register, but not s0..s11
      add  s2, s2, a0
      addi s0, s0, 8
      j    1b
  2:
      mv   a0, s2
      ld   s2, 0(sp)
      ld   s1, 8(sp)
      ld   s0, 16(sp)
      ld   ra, 24(sp)
      addi sp, sp, 32
      ret

When you read compiler output for a function with calls inside a loop, the first thing to identify is which s register holds which loop variable. After that the loop reads easily.

More than eight arguments, and structs

Arguments 9 and beyond are passed on the stack, at 0(sp), 8(sp), and so on, at the moment of the call. Small structs (up to 16 bytes on RV64) are passed in one or two a registers. Bigger structs are passed as a pointer to a copy. Return values bigger than two registers are written into memory that the caller provides, with its address passed as a hidden first argument.

The frame pointer

Unoptimized code (-O0) sets up s0 as a frame pointer: it points at the top of the current frame, and every local variable is accessed at a fixed negative offset from it, like -24(s0). This makes debugging easy and code slow. Chapter 8 shows a real -O0 listing. Optimized code usually drops the frame pointer and keeps locals in registers.

Exercises

  1. Why does square not need to save ra, but sum_squares does?
  2. In fib, could you keep n in t0 instead of s0? Explain exactly what breaks.
  3. Write long sum_rec(long *a, long n) recursively: 0 if n == 0, else a[0] + sum_rec(a + 1, n - 1). Draw its stack for n = 2.
  4. A function needs to save ra, s0, s1, s2 and s3. How many bytes does it reserve, and why?
  5. Some functions end with a call followed immediately by ret. A compiler can replace that pair with a plain jump to the callee (a tail call). Why is that correct, and what happens to the stack frame?

title: Whole programs: directives, syscalls, linking, encoding
html:
So far every example was a function called from somewhere else. This chapter covers what a complete assembly file contains, how a program talks to the operating system, how files are combined, and how one instruction is encoded as bits.

Directives

Lines starting with . are directives. They are instructions to the assembler, not to the CPU. They produce no machine instruction themselves.

DirectiveMeaning
.byte 1, 2, .half, .word, .dwordEmit 1, 2, 4 or 8-byte values
.ascii "hi" / .asciz "hi"Emit the bytes of a string (.asciz adds a zero
byte)
Pad with zeros until the address is a multiple of
2^3 = 8
Define a constant for the assembler
.text

.data

.rodata

.bss

.globl name
.align 3
.set name, value

A label like msg: or loop: is just a name for the address where the next byte will go. Code labels and data labels are the same kind of thing.

A complete program

This program prints one line and exits. It has no C, no library, nothing. It was run in the emulator, which captured exactly the bytes written:

hello.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # a whole program: print a message, then exit with status 0
  # linux on risc-v: syscall number in a7, arguments in a0..a5, then ecall
      .section .rodata
  msg:
      .ascii "hello from risc-v\n"
      .set len, . - msg     # len = current address minus start of msg

      .text
      .globl _start
  _start:
      li   a0, 1
                          # fd 1 = standard output
      la   a1, msg        # a1 = address of the bytes
      li   a2, len        # a2 = number of bytes
      li   a7, 64
                          # syscall 64 = write
      ecall
      li   a0, 0
                          # exit status
      li   a7, 93
                          # syscall 93 = exit
      ecall

. - msg means “the current address minus the address of msg”, which is the number of bytes in the string. The assembler computes it.

System calls

A program cannot write to the screen or a file by itself. It asks the operating system with a system call. On Linux on RISC-V, the rules are: put the syscall number in a7, the arguments in a0 to a5, then run ecall. The kernel takes over, does the work, puts the result in a0, and returns to the instruction after ecall.

SyscallNumber on RISC-V LinuxArguments
64A0 = file descriptor, a1 =
address of bytes, a2 = count
93A0 = exit status
63A0 = fd, a1 = buffer address,
a2 = max count
write
exit

read

The numbers are different on x86-64 Linux (write is 1, exit is 60, chapter 9). Every function in the C library that touches the outside world (printf, fopen, malloc for big blocks) ends in system calls like these.

Building and running it yourself

On an Ubuntu x86 machine, after sudo apt install gcc-riscv64-linux-gnu qemu-user:

riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc -nostdlib -static hello.s -o hello
qemu-riscv64 ./hello

-nostdlib means “do not link the C library or its startup code”. The program starts at _start, the default entry label. qemu-riscv64 runs a RISC-V Linux program on your x86 machine by translating its instructions.

To call your assembly functions from C (the easiest way to test them):

riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc -static test.c sum.s -o test
qemu-riscv64 ./test

Where test.c declares long sum(long *a, long n); and calls it.

Object files, symbols and relocations

The assembler cannot always finish its job. In fact.s, call fact jumps to a label in the same file, but a call to a function in another file has an unknown target. So the assembler writes a placeholder instruction and a relocation: a note saying “when the address of this symbol is known, patch these bits here”. The linker collects all object files, decides where everything goes in memory, and applies every relocation.

The symbol table lists every label marked .globl, so the linker can match a call in one file to a definition in another. nm file.o prints it. objdump -d file.o disassembles the code. objdump -r file.o shows the relocations still waiting to be filled in.

How an instruction is encoded

Every RISC-V instruction is 32 bits, split into fields. Arithmetic between registers uses the r- type layout:

The bits above are add t0, t1, t2. Read them left to right and group by 4: 0000 0000 0111 0011 0000 0010 1011 0011 = 0x007302b3. The assembler printed exactly this (as bytes in memory order, little endian: b3 02 73 00).

The opcode field says which family the instruction belongs to. funct3 and funct7 pick the exact operation inside the family: sub is the same as add except funct7 is 0100000. Each register field is 5 bits, because 2^5 = 32 registers.

An instruction with an immediate uses the i-type layout: the 12 bits that held funct7 and rs2 hold the immediate instead. That is where the 12-bit limit on immediates comes from: it is a direct consequence of fitting everything into 32 bits. Loads use i-type (ld t3, 8(a0) stores the 8 in those 12 bits). Branches and stores split their immediate across the fields in a scrambled-looking order, chosen so that the hardware can keep register fields in the same position in every format. That keeps the decoding circuit small and fast.

x86 instructions, by contrast, are anywhere from 1 to 15 bytes long, which makes decoding much harder for the chip. Chapter 9 shows examples.

Exercises

  1. Change hello.s to print two different lines with two write calls.
  2. Write a program that exits with status 42. Check it with echo $? after running it.
  3. sub t0, t1, t2 differs from add t0, t1, t2 only in funct7. What is its 32-bit encoding in hex?
  4. What is the largest forward distance a jal can jump, given that its immediate is 20 bits and counts in units of 2 bytes?

title: Reading compiler output
html:
This is the skill you will use most. Almost nobody writes large programs in assembly. People read what the compiler produced to find out why code is slow, whether an optimization happened, or what a crash means. This chapter teaches you to recognize what the compiler did to your code.

The workflow

  1. Put a small function into godbolt.org (or run clang -O2 -S file.c -o -).
  2. Pick the target and flags you care about. For RISC-V: --target=riscv64 -march=rv64im -O2.
  3. Find the loop. It is the label that a branch near the bottom jumps back to.
  4. For each register in the loop, write down which source variable it holds.
  5. Count the instructions in the loop body. That is the work per iteration.

The same function, unoptimized

This is the sum function from chapter 4, compiled by clang for RISC-V with -O0 (no optimization). It is real compiler output:

long sum(long *a, long n) {
    long s = 0;
    for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) s += a[i];
    return s;
}
compiler output: clang, risc-v rv64im

  sum:
          addi    sp, sp, -48
          sd      ra, 40(sp)
          sd      s0, 32(sp)
          addi    s0, sp, 48
          sd      a0, -24(s0)
          sd      a1, -32(s0)
          li      a0, 0
          sd      a0, -40(s0)
          sd      a0, -48(s0)
          j       .LBB0_1
  .LBB0_1:
          ld      a0, -48(s0)
          ld      a1, -32(s0)
          bge     a0, a1, .LBB0_4
          j       .LBB0_2
  .LBB0_2:
          ld      a0, -24(s0)
          ld      a1, -48(s0)
          slli    a1, a1, 3
          add     a0, a0, a1
          ld      a1, 0(a0)
          ld      a0, -40(s0)
          add     a0, a0, a1
          sd      a0, -40(s0)
          j       .LBB0_3
  .LBB0_3:
          ld      a0, -48(s0)
          addi    a0, a0, 1
          sd      a0, -48(s0)
          j       .LBB0_1
  .LBB0_4:
          ld      a0, -40(s0)
          ld      ra, 40(sp)
          ld      s0, 32(sp)
          addi    sp, sp, 48
          ret

At -O0 the compiler gives every variable a home on the stack and loads and stores it around every single use. S0 is the frame pointer. The four variables live at fixed offsets: a at -24(s0), n at -32(s0), s at -40(s0), i at -48(s0). One iteration of the loop does 7 loads (only one of them is the array element) and 2 stores, just to update two numbers.

Nobody ships -O0 code. It exists so a debugger can show you every variable at every line. Never judge performance from it.

The same function, optimized

With -O2:

compiler output: clang, risc-v rv64im

  sum:
          li      a2, 0
          blez    a1, .LBB0_3
          slli    a1, a1, 3
          add     a1, a0, a1
  .LBB0_2:
          ld      a3, 0(a0)
          addi    a0, a0, 8
          add     a2, a3, a2
          bne     a0, a1, .LBB0_2
  .LBB0_3:
          mv      a0, a2
          ret

8 instructions in total, 4 in the loop. Compare with the hand-written versions in chapter 4: the compiler arrived at the pointer-walking version on its own. Reading this, map each register:

  • a0 = the pointer, moving forward by 8 each iteration.
  • a1 = the end address: slli and add turned n into a + n*8.
  • a2 = s, the running sum.
  • a3 = the loaded element.

The blez a1 before the loop is the loop rotation from chapter 5: test once whether n is at most 0, and if so skip straight to returning 0. Then the loop tests at the bottom with bne.

Optimizations to recognize

These show up in almost every function you read. Learn their shapes.

NameWhat it doesWhat you see
Strength reductionReplaces expensive ops withi * 8 becomes a shift, or a
cheap onespointer that adds 8 each step
Induction variableRemoves a loop counter thatNo i at all; the loop stops
eliminationcan be derived from anotherwhen the pointer hits the end
Loop rotationMoves the loop test to theOne test before the loop, one
bottombranch at the end of the body
Constant foldingComputes constant expressions
at compile time		60 * 60 * 24 appears as
InliningCopies a small function’s bodyA call you expected is
into its callermissing; its work appears in
place
Dead code eliminationDeletes work whose result isA computation you wrote is
never usedsimply gone
Tail callcall f; ret becomes j fA function ends in a jump to
another function
UnrollingRepeats the loop body k times4 or 8 copies of the body,
per iterationpointer steps of 32 or 64
VectorizationUses SIMD registers to doWide registers and instructions
several elements at once(chapter 10)
86400

“the compiler deleted my benchmark” is the most common beginner surprise, and dead code elimination is why. If you compute something and never use the result, the loop is removed. Benchmarks in this book write results into a volatile variable to prevent that.

Multiplying and dividing by constants

Compilers avoid multiply and divide instructions when the constant is known. This is real x86-64 output (Intel syntax, which chapter 9 explains in full; rdi is the argument and rax is the result):

long mul5add3(long x) { return x * 5 + 3; }
long div8(long x)
                      { return x / 8; }
unsigned long udiv8(unsigned long x) { return x / 8; }
long div7(long x)
                      { return x / 7; }
compiler output: clang, x86-64, intel syntax

  mul5add3:
          lea     rax, [rdi + 4*rdi]
          add     rax, 3
          ret
  div8:
          lea     rax, [rdi + 7]
          test
                  rdi, rdi
          cmovns
                  rax, rdi
          sar
                  rax, 3
          ret
  udiv8:
          mov     rax, rdi
          shr
                  rax, 3
          ret
  div7:
          mov     rax, rdi
          movabs  rcx, 5270498306774157605
          imul
                  rcx
          mov     rax, rdx
          shr
                  rax, 63
          sar
                  rdx
          add     rax, rdx
          ret

Line by line:

  • mul5add3: lea rax, [rdi + 4*rdi] computes x + 4x = 5x using the address-calculation hardware, without touching memory. Then add 3. No multiply instruction.
  • udiv8: unsigned division by 8 is one right shift by 3.
  • div8: signed division must round toward zero, but a shift rounds toward negative infinity (chapter 1). The fix: if x is negative, add 7 first. lea rax, [rdi + 7] computes x + 7, test and cmovns pick x instead when x is not negative, then sar shifts. No branch.
  • div7: division by 7 cannot be done with shifts. Instead the compiler multiplies by a “magic number” close to 2^65 / 7 and keeps the top bits of the 128-bit product. imul rcx with one operand multiplies rax by rcx into the 128-bit pair rdx:rax, so rdx holds the top 64 bits, which is x × m / 2^64. sar rdx shifts once more (total: divide by 2^65). The shr rax, 63 and add add 1 when x is negative, to round toward zero. A division instruction takes 10 to 40+ cycles; this sequence takes a handful.

When you see a giant constant and a multiply where your code had a division, this is what it is.

Bounds checks in Rust

Rust checks every slice index at run time. Here is real rustc output (-C opt-level=3, x86-64) for a loop that indexes with values coming from another slice. The panic path’s long internal name has been shortened:

pub fn get_sum(a: &[i64], idx: &[usize]) -> i64 {
    let mut s = 0;
    for &i in idx { s += a[i]; }
    s
}
compiler output: rustc -C opt-level=3, x86-64

  get_sum:
          test
                  rcx, rcx
          je      .LBB0_1
          shl
                  rcx, 3
          xor
                  eax, eax
          xor
                  r9d, r9d
  .LBB0_3:
          mov     r8, qword ptr [rdx + r9]
          cmp     r8, rsi
          jae     .LBB0_6
          add     rax, qword ptr [rdi + 8*r8]
          add     r9, 8
          cmp     rcx, r9
          jne     .LBB0_3
          ret
  .LBB0_1:
          xor
                  eax, eax
          ret
  .LBB0_6:
          push
                  rax
          lea     rdx, [rip + .Lpanic_location]
          mov     rdi, r8
          call    qword ptr [rip + core::panicking::panic_bounds_check@GOTPCREL]

A slice is passed as two registers: the pointer and the length. So a arrives as rdi (pointer) and rsi (length), and idx as rdx and rcx. Inside the loop, cmp r8, rsi / jae .LBB0_6 is the bounds check: if the index is above or equal to the length (unsigned compare), jump to the panic. It costs a compare and a branch per element, and the branch is always predicted correctly, so it is cheap here. The real cost is elsewhere: a loop containing a possible panic usually cannot be vectorized, because the vector version would have to know which exact element panicked.

When the compiler can prove the index is in range (for example when you iterate with for &x in a), the check disappears. Writing Rust loops with iterators instead of indices is how you get those checks removed.

Exercises

  1. Compile the max function from chapter 4 in C with -O2 for RISC-V on godbolt. Compare it with your hand-written version. Which registers hold which variables?
  2. Compile long f(long x) { return x * 9; } and x * 10 for x86-64. What instructions appear instead of imul?
  3. Compile unsigned div10(unsigned x) { return x / 10; }. Find the magic number. Compute magic × 1000 by hand (or in Python) and check the top bits give 100.
  4. Write a C function where the result of a loop is never used. Compile it with -O2. What remains?

title: x86-64 for someone who knows RISC-V
html:
x86-64 is what runs on almost every server, desktop and Windows laptop. Its history goes back to the Intel 8086 from 1978, and it carries that history in its register names, its encoding, and some odd rules. But the ideas are the ones you already know from RISC-V: registers, loads, stores, branches, a stack, a calling convention. This chapter maps each idea across.

The registers

There are 16 general registers of 64 bits. The first eight have historical names, the last eight are just numbered:

64-bitLow 32 bitsLow 16Low 8Historical role
r8.. r15r8d.. r15dr8w..r8b..(Added in 2003)
rax
                 eax
                                  ax
                                                   al
rbx
                 ebx
                                  bx
                                                   bl

rcx
                 ecx
                                  cx
                                                   cl
rdx
                 edx
                                  dx
                                                   dl
rsi
                 esi
                                  si
                                                   sil

rdi
                 edi
                                  di
                                                   dil

rbp
                 ebp
                                  bp
                                                   bpl
rsp
                 esp
                                  sp
                                                   spl

The smaller names are not separate registers. eax is the low 32 bits of rax. One rule here prevents real bugs: writing a 32-bit register zeroes the upper 32 bits, but writing an 8 or 16-bit register leaves the upper bits unchanged. That is why compilers write xor eax, eax to zero all of rax: it is shorter to encode than xor rax, rax and does the same thing.

There is no zero register like RISC-V’s x0. pc is called rip (instruction pointer). There is also rflags, a register of status bits set by arithmetic, explained below.

Two syntaxes

x86 assembly is written in two different text formats for the same instructions. This is pure notation, the machine code is identical. Intel syntax (used by Intel’s manuals, Windows tools, and this book) puts the destination first like RISC-V. At&t syntax (the default for gcc, objdump and gdb on Linux) puts it last and adds symbols:

IntelAt&t
add rax, rbx
                             addq %rbx, %rax

mov rax, qword ptr [rdi +
                             movq (%rdi,%rcx,8), %rax8*rcx]

Constant

mov eax, 1
                             movl $1, %eax

To get Intel syntax: clang -S -masm=intel, objdump -d -M intel, and in gdb set disassembly-flavor intel. On godbolt it is the default.

Two operands, not three

Most x86 arithmetic has two operands, and the first is both a source and the destination:

add  rax, rbx        # rax = rax + rbx      (risc-v would need: add a0, a0, a1)
sub  rax, 5          # rax = rax - 5
imul rax, rcx        # rax = rax * rcx
mov  rax, rbx        # rax = rbx            (copy)

So to compute c = a + b without destroying a, the compiler first copies: mov rcx, rax then add rcx, rbx, or uses lea (below).

Memory operands

The big difference from RISC-V: most instructions can read or write one operand directly in memory. The address can be:

[base + index*scale + displacement]       scale is 1, 2, 4 or 8

So add rax, qword ptr [rdi + 8*rcx] loads a[i] (with rdi = a, rcx = i) and adds it to rax, in one instruction. The qword ptr says the memory operand is 8 bytes. This addressing form covers array indexing directly, which is why x86 loops often have fewer instructions than RISC-V loops. Inside the chip, the instruction is still split into a load and an add.

Lea: arithmetic with the address hardware

lea (load effective address) computes the address expression and puts the address itself in the register. It does not touch memory. Compilers use it as a free three-operand add and small multiply:

lea  rax, [rdi + 4*rdi]     # rax = 5 * rdi
lea  rax, [rdi + rsi]       # rax = rdi + rsi, without destroying either
lea  rsi, [rip + msg]       # rsi = address of label msg (position independent)

Flags and conditional jumps

RISC-V branches compare two registers directly. x86 splits this into two steps. Arithmetic instructions and cmp set bits in rflags. A conditional jump then reads those bits.

cmp  rcx, rsi        # compute rcx - rsi, set flags, throw the result away
jge  done            # jump if the result said rcx >= rsi (signed)

test rsi, rsi computes rsi & rsi, sets flags, and discards the result. It is the standard way to check if a register is zero or negative.

JumpSigned or unsigned
je / jne
A == b / a != b		Either
jl / jge
A < b / a >= b		Signed (less, greater)
jg / jle
A > b / a <= b		Signed
jb / jae
A < b / a >= b		Unsigned (below, above)
ja / jbe
A > b / a <= b		Unsigned
js / jns
Result negative / not negative		Sign bit

Meaning after cmp a, b

The Rust bounds check in chapter 8 used jae: an unsigned compare, so a “negative” index looks huge and also fails the check. One compare covers both cases.

Flags also drive cmovcc (conditional move, no branch) and setcc (write 0 or 1 into a byte register).

The calling convention (system v, Linux and Mac)

RoleRegisters
Arguments 1 to 6rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9
Float argumentsxmm0 to xmm7
Return valuerax (and rdx); floats in xmm0
Callee-savedrbx, rbp, r12, r13, r14, r15
Caller-savedEverything else

Windows uses a different convention (rcx, rdx, r8, r9 for the first four arguments). If your assembly must run on both, you need two versions.

call f pushes the return address onto the stack (subtract 8 from rsp, store rip there) and jumps. ret pops it back into rip. So unlike RISC-V, the return address lives on the stack, not in a register. push rbx stores a register on the stack and moves rsp down by 8. pop rbx does the reverse.

One more rule: rsp must be a multiple of 16 at every call . Since call pushes 8 bytes, a function starts with rsp ending in 8, and must move rsp by an odd multiple of 8 before it calls anything.

The examples again

The array sum, hand-written in Intel syntax and tested natively against C:

sum.s · x86-64, run and checked natively

  # long sum(long *a, long n)     intel syntax, linux / system v abi
  # rdi = a, rsi = n, return value in rax
      .intel_syntax noprefix
      .globl sum
  sum:
      xor
           eax, eax
                                  # rax = s = 0 (writing eax also zeroes the top half)xor
           ecx, ecx
                                  # rcx = i = 0
  .Lloop:
      cmp  rcx, rsi
                                  # compare i with n, sets flags
      jge  .Ldone                 # jump if i >= n (reads the flags)
      add  rax, qword ptr [rdi + rcx*8]
                                          # s += a[i], load and add in one instructioninc
           rcx
                                  # i++
      jmp  .Lloop
  .Ldone:
      ret

And what clang produces with -O2 (vectorization turned off so the scalar loop is visible):

compiler output: clang, x86-64, intel syntax

  sum:
          test
                  rsi, rsi
          jle     .LBB0_1
          xor
                  ecx, ecx
          xor
                  eax, eax
  .LBB0_4:
          add     rax, qword ptr [rdi + 8*rcx]
          inc
                  rcx
          cmp     rsi, rcx
          jne     .LBB0_4
          ret
  .LBB0_1:
          xor
                  eax, eax
          ret

The loop is 4 instructions: one add-from-memory, one increment, one compare, one branch. Note the compiler compares rsi with rcx at the bottom (loop rotation again) and checks test rsi, rsi / jle before the loop.

Max, using a conditional move instead of a branch:

max.s · x86-64, run and checked natively

  # long max(long *a, long n), n >= 1, no branch for the update: cmov
      .intel_syntax noprefix
      .globl max
  max:
      mov  rax, qword ptr [rdi]
                                  # best = a[0]
      mov  ecx, 1
                                  # i = 1
  .Lloop:
      cmp  rcx, rsi
      jge  .Ldone
      mov  rdx, qword ptr [rdi + rcx*8]
                                          # rdx = a[i]
      cmp  rdx, rax
                                  # flags = compare a[i] with best
      cmovg rax, rdx
                                  # if a[i] > best: best = a[i]   (no jump)
      inc
           rcx
      jmp  .Lloop
  .Ldone:
      ret

Recursive factorial, using push and pop to save the callee-saved register rbx:

fact.s · x86-64, run and checked natively

  # long fact(long n), recursive, shows push/pop and the call stack
      .intel_syntax noprefix
      .globl fact
  fact:
      cmp  rdi, 1
      jg   .Lrec
      mov  eax, 1
                                  # base case
      ret
  .Lrec:
      push rbx
                                  # rbx is callee-saved: save the caller's value
      mov  rbx, rdi
                                  # rbx = n, survives the call
      lea  rdi, [rdi - 1]
                                  # argument = n - 1
      call fact                   # pushes the return address, jumps
      imul rax, rbx
                                  # rax = fact(n - 1) * n
      pop
           rbx
                                  # restore the caller's rbx
      ret
                                  # pops the return address into rip

Check the alignment rule here: on entry rsp ends in 8. push rbx moves it by 8, so it is a multiple of 16 at call fact. This one push both saves rbx and fixes alignment. You will see compilers push a register they do not even need just to align the stack.

A whole program, with Linux x86-64 syscall numbers (write = 1, exit = 60) and the syscall instruction:

hello.s · x86-64, run and checked natively

  # whole program for linux x86-64: write, then exit
  # syscall number in rax, arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, then the syscall instruction.intel_syntax noprefix
      .section .rodata
  msg:
      .ascii "hello from x86-64\n"
      .set len, . - msg
      .text
      .globl _start
  _start:
      mov  eax, 1
                                  # syscall 1 = write
      mov  edi, 1
                                  # fd 1 = stdout
      lea  rsi, [rip + msg]
                                  # address of msg, relative to this instruction
      mov  edx, len
      syscall
      mov  eax, 60
                                  # syscall 60 = exit
      xor
           edi, edi
                                  # status 0
      syscall

Variable-length encoding

x86 instructions are 1 to 15 bytes long. Real encodings from the assembler:

ret                                  c3                            1 byte
add rax, rbx                         48 01 d8                      3 bytes
add rax, qword ptr [rdi + 8*rcx]     48 03 04 cf                   4 bytes
mov rax, 0x123456789abcdef0          48 b8 f0 de bc 9a 78 56 34 12 10 bytes
vfmadd231ps ymm7, ymm10, ymm8        c4 c2 2d b8 f8                5 bytes

The 48 byte at the start of several of these is a prefix meaning “64-bit operands”. The chip must find where each instruction ends before it can decode the next one, which is real work. Modern x86 cores keep a cache of already-decoded instructions to avoid repeating it for hot loops.

Exercises

  1. Translate the RISC-V rev function (chapter 5) into x86-64 Intel syntax.
  2. What is in rax after mov rax, -1 followed by mov eax, 5? And after mov rax, -1 then mov al, 5?
  3. Write long dot(long *a, long *b, long n) in x86-64.
  4. Why does cmp followed by jae catch both “index too large” and “index negative” when the index is a signed number?
  5. A function pushes rbx and r12 and then calls another function. Is the stack aligned at the call? What if it pushed only rbx and r12 and r13?

title: SIMD: one instruction, many numbers
html:
SIMD means single instruction, multiple data. A SIMD register holds several numbers side by side, called lanes, and one instruction does the same operation on every lane at once. If a register holds 8 floats, one add does 8 additions in the time a normal add does one. This is the first big source of speed on a CPU, and the same idea, scaled up, is what a GPU is.

The registers

Floats (f32)Longs (i64) perInstruction
Name
Width
per registerregisterset
xmm0.. xmm15
128 bits
4		2SSE (every
x86-64 chip)
ymm0.. ymm15
256 bits
8		4AVX, AVX2
zmm0.. zmm31
512 bits
16		8AVX-512 (some
Intel and AMD
chips)

Xmm0 is the low half of ymm0, which is the low half of zmm0. Scalar float math on x86-64 also uses xmm registers, using only the lowest lane.

Arm has NEON (128-bit) and SVE. RISC-V has the “v” extension, where the vector length is decided by the chip and the code asks for it at run time. The ideas in this chapter apply to all of them.

Reading the instruction names

SIMD instruction names are built from parts:

  • v prefix: the AVX encoding (three operands, like RISC-V).
  • The operation: add, mul, fmadd, mov, broadcast, …
  • For floats, the last two letters: ps = packed single (all f32 lanes), pd = packed double (all f64 lanes), ss = scalar single (only lane 0), sd = scalar double.
  • For integers, a p prefix and a size suffix: vpaddq = packed add of qwords (64-bit lanes), vpaddd = 32-bit lanes.

So vaddps ymm0, ymm1, ymm2 adds 8 pairs of floats. vaddss xmm0, xmm1, xmm2 adds one pair. When you read compiler output and want to know if a loop was vectorized, look for ps and ymm instead of ss and xmm.

FMA: fused multiply-add

vfmadd231ps ymm7, ymm10, ymm8 computes ymm7 = ymm10 * ymm8 + ymm7 on 8 lanes, with only one rounding at the end. The digits say which operands are multiplied and which is added: in 231, operand 2 times operand 3, plus operand 1. FMA is the core instruction of all of linear algebra and ML: a dot product, a matrix multiply and a convolution are long chains of multiply-add. One FMA on 8 lanes is 16 floating point operations (8 multiplies and 8 adds).

A vectorized integer sum

The sum function from earlier, compiled by clang with -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 (allowing AVX2). Unrolling was limited to one vector per iteration so the structure is clear:

compiler output: clang, x86-64, intel syntax

  sum:
          test
                  rsi, rsi
          jle     .LBB0_1
          cmp     rsi, 4
          jae     .LBB0_4
          xor
                  ecx, ecx
          xor
                  eax, eax
          jmp     .LBB0_7
  .LBB0_1:
          xor
                  eax, eax
          ret
  .LBB0_4:
          movabs  rcx, 9223372036854775804
          and
                  rcx, rsi
          vpxor
                  xmm0, xmm0, xmm0
          xor
                  eax, eax
  .LBB0_5:
          vpaddq
                  ymm0, ymm0, ymmword ptr [rdi + 8*rax]
          add     rax, 4
          cmp     rcx, rax
          jne     .LBB0_5
          vextracti128
                          xmm1, ymm0, 1
          vpaddq
                  xmm0, xmm0, xmm1
          vpshufd xmm1, xmm0, 238
                                                  # xmm1 = xmm0[2,3,2,3]
          vpaddq
                  xmm0, xmm0, xmm1
          vmovq
                  rax, xmm0
          cmp     rcx, rsi
          je      .LBB0_8
  .LBB0_7:
          add     rax, qword ptr [rdi + 8*rcx]
          inc
                  rcx
          cmp     rsi, rcx
          jne     .LBB0_7
  .LBB0_8:
          vzeroupper
          ret

There are three parts, and you will see this three-part shape in nearly every vectorized loop:

  1. The main vector loop (.LBB0_5): vpaddq ymm0, ymm0, ymmword ptr [rdi + 8*rax] loads 4 longs (32 bytes) and adds them to 4 running sums in ymm0. The counter goes up by 4. Before the loop, movabs rcx, ... and and rcx, rsi round n down to a multiple of 4. That constant is 0x7ffffffffffffffc: all ones except the low two bits.
  2. The horizontal reduction: after the loop, ymm0 holds 4 partial sums that must be added together. vextracti128 takes the upper 128 bits, vpaddq adds them to the lower half (now 2 sums), vpshufd moves the upper 64 bits down, vpaddq again (now 1 sum), vmovq copies it to rax.
  3. The scalar tail (.LBB0_7): the last n mod 4 elements, one at a time. This is the old scalar loop.

vzeroupper at the end is a housekeeping instruction that avoids a slowdown when mixing AVX and older SSE code. It does no math.

Why the compiler can reorder integers but not floats

Look at what the vectorized sum really does: it adds elements 0, 4, 8, … into lane 0, elements 1, 5, 9, … into lane 1, and so on, then combines the lanes at the end. That is a different order of additions than the C code. For integers this gives the same result, because integer addition (with wraparound) is associative.

For floats it would not (chapter 1: float addition is not associative). So for a float sum, clang and gcc will not vectorize the reduction unless you pass -ffast-math (or -fassociative-math), or write the multiple accumulators yourself. Chapter 11 measures what that costs.

A vectorized saxpy

Saxpy is y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i]. There is no reduction here: each element is independent. So the compiler vectorizes it without any special flags:

void saxpy(float *restrict y, const float *restrict x, float a, long n) {
    for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i];
}
compiler output: clang, x86-64, intel syntax

  saxpy:
          test
                  rdx, rdx
          jle     .LBB0_7
          cmp     rdx, 8
          jae     .LBB0_3
          xor
                  eax, eax
          jmp     .LBB0_6
  .LBB0_3:
          movabs  rax, 9223372036854775800
          and
                  rax, rdx
          vbroadcastss
                          ymm1, xmm0
          xor
                  ecx, ecx
  .LBB0_4:
          vmovups ymm2, ymmword ptr [rsi + 4*rcx]
          vfmadd213ps
                          ymm2, ymm1, ymmword ptr [rdi + 4*rcx]
  # ymm2 = (ymm1 * ymm2) + mem
          vmovups ymmword ptr [rdi + 4*rcx], ymm2
          add     rcx, 8
          cmp     rax, rcx
          jne     .LBB0_4
          cmp     rax, rdx
          je      .LBB0_7
  .LBB0_6:
          vmovss
                  xmm1, dword ptr [rsi + 4*rax]
          vfmadd213ss
                          xmm1, xmm0, dword ptr [rdi + 4*rax]
  # xmm1 = (xmm0 * xmm1) + mem
          vmovss  dword ptr [rdi + 4*rax], xmm1
          inc
                  rax
          cmp     rdx, rax
          jne     .LBB0_6
  .LBB0_7:
          vzeroupper
          ret

vbroadcastss ymm1, xmm0 copies the scalar a (passed in xmm0) into all 8 lanes of ymm1. Then the main loop processes 8 floats per iteration: load 8 of x, FMA with 8 of y from memory, store 8 back. The tail loop does the same with ss instructions, one element at a time.

Restrict and aliasing

The restrict keyword in saxpy promises the compiler that x and y do not overlap in memory. Without that promise, the compiler must assume writing y[i] might change x[i+1], which would make loading 8 values of x ahead of time wrong. It then either refuses to vectorize or adds a run-time check comparing the two pointers and keeps two versions of the loop. Rust slices give the compiler this guarantee automatically (a &mut slice cannot overlap anything else), which is one reason Rust loops vectorize well.

What blocks vectorization

When a loop does not vectorize, it is usually one of these:

  • A float reduction without permission to reorder.
  • Possible aliasing between pointers.
  • A loop-carried dependency: iteration i needs the result of iteration i - 1 (like a prefix sum).
  • A possible early exit: a break, a panic, an out-of-bounds check.
  • Non-contiguous access: a[idx[i]] (a gather) or a large stride.
  • A function call inside the loop that was not inlined.

clang tells you why with -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize. gcc has -fopt-info-vec-missed.

Exercises

  1. Compile saxpy without restrict on godbolt. What changes in the output?
  2. Compile the float version of sum (float sum(float *a, long n)) with -O3 -march=x86-64-v3, then add -ffast-math. Compare the loops.
  3. In the vectorized sum, what happens when n = 3? Trace which parts of the code run.
  4. How many floating point operations does one vfmadd231ps on zmm registers do?

title: The cost model
html:
Assembly tells you what work a program asks for. This chapter is about how long that work takes. The short version: on a modern chip, arithmetic is almost free, and the time goes into waiting. Waiting for memory, waiting for a previous result, waiting after a wrong guess. Every number in this chapter was measured on the machine that built this book. They will be different on yours. The ratios will not be far off.

Cycles, latency and throughput

The CPU runs on a clock. One tick is a cycle. At 3 GHz a cycle is a third of a nanosecond.

A modern core does not run one instruction at a time. It is pipelined (each instruction passes through many stages, and different instructions occupy different stages at the same moment) and superscalar (it can start several instructions per cycle). Two numbers describe each kind of instruction:

  • Latency: cycles from when an instruction starts until its result can be used by the next instruction.
  • Throughput: how many of that instruction the core can start per cycle, when they do not depend on each other.

Typical numbers for recent x86 cores (they vary by chip; exact tables are at uops.info):

OperationLatency (cycles)Can start per cycle
Integer add, logic, shift13 to 4
Integer multiply31
Float add / multiply / FMA2 to 42
Integer divide (64-bit)About 10 to 40+Much less than 1
Load that hits L1 cache4 to 52 to 3
Branch, correctly predicted(None visible)1 to 2
Branch, mispredictedAbout 15 to 20 lost

The two columns tell different stories. A float add takes several cycles to finish, but the core can start two new ones every cycle. If each add needs the previous add’s result, you get one add per several cycles. If the adds are independent, you get two per cycle. The difference is up to 8x, from the same instruction.

Dependency chains

Here is that effect measured. Three functions sum the same 4096 floats (16 KB, which fits in L1 cache, so memory is not the issue). The first uses one accumulator, so every add waits for the previous one. The others split the work into 4 or 8 independent accumulators. Compiled with -O2 and no vectorization, so each add is a scalar addss:

float sum1(const float *x) {
                                           // one chain
    float s = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) s += x[i];
    return s;
}
float sum4(const float *x) {
                                           // four independent chains
    float s0 = 0, s1 = 0, s2 = 0, s3 = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i += 4) { s0 += x[i]; s1 += x[i+1]; s2 += x[i+2]; s3 +=x[i+3]; }
    return (s0 + s1) + (s2 + s3);
}

Measured:

measured output

  1 chain   0.694 ns per element
  4 chains  0.174 ns per element
  8 chains  0.164 ns per element

Four chains are 4x faster than one. The work is identical: the same number of loads and adds. The only change is that four adds can be in flight at once instead of one. Eight chains are no faster than four, because by then the core is already doing about two loads and two adds every cycle, its throughput limit. Once you hit throughput, more independence does not help.

This is the exact reason a compiler cannot speed up sum1 itself: splitting into four chains changes the order of float additions, which can change the result (chapter 1). You must either write the chains yourself or allow reordering with -ffast-math. ML compilers (tinygrad, Triton, TVM) do the same thing when they split a reduction into several accumulators; tinygrad calls it “upcasting”. It is the same trick on a GPU.

Out-of-order execution

A modern core looks ahead in the instruction stream, a window of hundreds of instructions, and starts any instruction whose inputs are ready, regardless of program order. The results are still committed in program order, so the program cannot tell. This is how a core keeps busy while one load waits for memory: it runs independent later instructions in the meantime. It also means the order instructions appear in a listing is not the order they run. What limits speed is the chain of dependencies, not the instruction count.

Branch prediction

A pipelined core must fetch the instructions after a branch before it knows which way the branch goes. So it guesses, using the history of that branch. A correct guess costs almost nothing. A wrong guess means everything fetched after the branch is thrown away and the core restarts from the right address. That costs roughly 15 to 20 cycles.

Measured: the same loop over the same million values, adding only the values at least 128. On random data the branch goes each way about half the time, so the guess is wrong about half the time. On sorted data the branch goes one way for the first half and the other way for the second half, so the guess is almost always right:

measured output

  unsorted: 4.37 ns per element
  sorted:
            0.44 ns per element

A 10x difference for identical work. Now the compiler’s own version at -O2, which replaced the branch with a conditional move (cmovg):

measured output

  unsorted: 0.67 ns per element
  sorted:
            0.70 ns per element

The branchless version does not care about the data order. It is slower than a well-predicted branch (it always does the add) and much faster than a badly-predicted one. That is the rule: branchless code wins only when the branch is unpredictable.

Caches

Memory is far away. To hide that, the chip keeps copies of recently used memory in caches: small, fast memories close to the core. Data moves between memory and caches in fixed blocks of 64 bytes called cache lines. Reading one byte brings its whole 64-byte line into the cache.

There are usually three levels. On this machine: 48 KB of L1 data cache per core, 2 MB of L2 per core, and a large shared L3. To measure the latency of each, the benchmark builds a random chain of pointers through a block of memory of a given size, one pointer per cache line, and follows it. Each load gives the address of the next one, so the core cannot start load k + 1 before load k finishes. This measures pure latency:

16 KB fits in L1: 1.7 ns. 64 KB and 512 KB are in L2: about 6 ns. 16 MB lives in L3: 43 ns. 128 MB and up go to main memory: 140 to 170 ns. The gap between L1 and main memory is 100x.

Now the same 512 MB, read in order instead of randomly, still one load per cache line:

measured output

  in-order, one load per cache line: 3.98 ns per line (16.1 GB/s)
                                                                   0

4 ns instead of 170 ns, from the same memory. Two things change. The loads no longer depend on each other, so many can be in flight. And the hardware prefetcher notices the sequential pattern and starts fetching lines before the program asks for them. The order you touch memory in matters as much as how much memory you touch.

The practical rules that follow:

  • Use every byte of a cache line you pay for. Walking an array in order uses all 64 bytes. Jumping around uses 8 of them.
  • Keep the data a loop works on small enough to stay in cache while the loop needs it. This is what “tiling” or “blocking” means.
  • Linked lists and trees of separately allocated nodes are slow because every step is a dependent load to a random address. Arrays are fast.
  • Memory is also split into 4 KB pages, and translating each page address is cached in the TLB. Random access over a huge range misses the TLB too, which adds to the cost you saw above.

Compute bound or memory bound

For any loop, compare two limits: how fast the core can do its arithmetic, and how fast memory can deliver its bytes. Arithmetic intensity is the number of floating point operations done per byte moved from memory.

Saxpy (y = a * x + y) loads 8 bytes and stores 4 per element and does 2 FLOPs: 2 / 12, about 0.17 FLOPs per byte. At 16 GB/s from memory, that is under 3 GFLOP/s, far below what one core’s FMA units can do. Saxpy is memory bound: faster arithmetic would not help at all.

A matrix multiply of two n × n matrices does 2n³ FLOPs on 3n² numbers. For n = 512 each number gets reused hundreds of times, so if the code is written to reuse data while it is in registers and cache, it can be compute bound. The next chapter shows how big that “if” is.

This way of thinking (plot FLOPs per second against FLOPs per byte, and see which limit you hit) is called the roofline model. It applies to GPUs without change, and it is the first question to ask about any kernel.

Measuring instead of guessing

  • perf stat ./program prints cycles, instructions, instructions per cycle (IPC), branch misses and cache misses. IPC tells you a lot: near 4 means the core is busy, below 1 means it is mostly waiting.
  • perf record ./program then perf report shows which functions take the time. perf annotate shows the hot instructions in the assembly itself, with the percentage of samples on each line. This is where reading assembly pays off directly.
  • llvm-mca takes a block of assembly and predicts its cycles per iteration on a chosen chip, showing which resource is the bottleneck. Useful for small hot loops.
  • uops.info and Agner fog’s instruction tables list latency and throughput per instruction per chip.

One warning: in perf annotate, the cost often shows up on the instruction after the slow one, because that is where the core was waiting when the sample was taken. A hot add right after a load usually means the load is the problem.

Exercises

  1. A loop does 1 million dependent float adds with a 4-cycle latency at 3 GHz. How long does it take at minimum? How long if the adds were split into 8 independent chains and the core can start 2 per cycle?
  2. Why is the pointer-chasing benchmark a measure of latency, and the in-order benchmark a measure of bandwidth?
  3. Compute the arithmetic intensity of a dot product of two float arrays. Is it compute bound or memory bound on this machine?
  4. Run perf stat -e branch-misses on the branch benchmark yourself (code in appendix C). How many misses per element do you expect for the unsorted case?

title: Case study: matrix multiply on a CPU
html:
This chapter puts everything together on the most important operation in ML. Three versions of C = A × B for 512 × 512 float matrices, the same math in each, timed on the same machine and compiled with clang -O3 -march=x86-64-v3. Then the assembly of the slowest and the fastest, so you can see exactly where the time went. This is exactly the work an ML compiler has to do automatically when it generates fast CPU kernels.

Three versions

#define N 512
float A[N][N], B[N][N], C[N][N];

// 1. textbook order
void mm_ijk(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
        float acc = 0;
        for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) acc += A[i][k] * B[k][j];
        C[i][j] = acc;
    }
}

// 2. loops swapped: the inner loop runs along rows of B and C
void mm_ikj(void) {
    memset(C, 0, sizeof C);
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
        float a = A[i][k];
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) C[i][j] += a * B[k][j];
    }
}

// 3. register tile: compute a 4 x 16 block of C at a time, kept in registers
void mm_tile(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i += 4) for (int j = 0; j < N; j += 16) {
        float acc[4][16] = {{0}};
        for (int k = 0; k < N; k++)
            for (int ii = 0; ii < 4; ii++)
                for (int jj = 0; jj < 16; jj++)
                    acc[ii][jj] += A[i+ii][k] * B[k][j+jj];
        for (int ii = 0; ii < 4; ii++) for (int jj = 0; jj < 16; jj++)
            C[i+ii][j+jj] = acc[ii][jj];
    }
}

Measured (one core; a 512³ multiply is 2 × 512³ ≈ 268 million FLOPs):

measured output

  ijk (textbook)
                   152.90 ms      1.8 GFLOP/s   ok
  ikj (swapped)
                     7.55 ms     35.6 GFLOP/s   ok
  4x16 reg tile      3.94 ms     68.1 GFLOP/s   ok

The fastest is about 38x faster than the textbook version. Same FLOPs, same answer (the “ok” column checks two output values against version 1).

Why the textbook version is slow

The inner loop of mm_ijk, real compiler output:

compiler output: clang, x86-64, intel syntax

  mm_ijk:
          lea     rax, [rip + A+28]

          lea     rsi, [rip + C]

          mov     rdi, rcx
          shl

          add     rdi, rsi

          vmovss
                  xmm1, dword ptr [rax + 4*r11 - 8]
          vfmadd132ss
                          xmm1, xmm0, dword ptr [r10 - 4096] # xmm1 = (xmm1 * mem) +xmm0
          vmovss
                  xmm2, dword ptr [rax + 4*r11 - 4]
          vfmadd132ss
                          xmm2, xmm1, dword ptr [r10 - 2048] # xmm2 = (xmm2 * mem) +xmm1
          vmovss
                  xmm0, dword ptr [rax + 4*r11]
          vfmadd132ss
                          xmm0, xmm2, dword ptr [r10] # xmm0 = (xmm0 * mem) + xmm2
          add     r11, 8
          add     r10, 16384
          cmp     r11, 512
          jne     .LBB0_3
          vmovss  dword ptr [rdi + 4*r9], xmm0
          inc
                  r9
          add     r8, 4
          cmp     r9, 512
          jne     .LBB0_2
          inc
                  rcx
          add     rax, 2048
          cmp     rcx, 512
          jne     .LBB0_1
          ret

Look at the innermost loop (.LBB0_3). Three problems are visible in the assembly:

  1. Scalar: every instruction ends in ss. One float at a time, using 1 of 8 lanes.
  2. One dependency chain: each vfmadd takes the previous one’s result (xmm0 feeds xmm1 feeds xmm0 …). This is sum1 from chapter 11 again. The compiler may not split it into several accumulators, because that would reorder float additions.
  3. Strided loads: the B operands are at [r10 - 14336], [r10 - 12288], … 2048 bytes apart. That is one row of B (512 floats × 4 bytes). Every B load touches a different cache line and uses 4 of its 64 bytes. Worse, addresses exactly 2048 bytes apart map to the same few sets of the cache and evict each other.

Why swapping the loops helps

In mm_ikj, the inner loop is C[i][j] += a * B[k][j] for j = 0..511. All three of the c-level problems disappear: the j loop walks rows of B and C, so loads are consecutive and use whole cache lines. Each C[i][j] is independent of the others, so there is no reduction chain. And the loop is saxpy, which chapter 10 showed vectorizes into 8-wide FMAs. That gives a 20x jump.

But it is still mostly memory bound: for every FMA on 8 floats, it loads 8 floats of B, loads 8 floats of C, and stores 8 floats of C. 3 memory operations per FMA.

The register tile

The tile version computes a 4 × 16 block of C. For each k it needs 4 values of A (one per row of the tile) and 16 values of B (one row segment), and it does 4 × 16 = 64 multiply-adds with them. Every A value is used 16 times and every B value 4 times before it leaves the registers. The accumulators never touch memory until the end. Real compiler output:

                                                  # ymm5 = (ymm10 * ymm8) + ymm5

          vbroadcastss
                          ymm10, dword ptr [rax + 4*r11 + 2048]

                                                  # ymm1 = (ymm10 * ymm8) + ymm1
          vfmadd231ps
