                                                  # ymm0 = (ymm10 * ymm9) + ymm0
          add     rbx, 2048
          inc
                  r11
          jne     .LBB2_3
          vmovups ymmword ptr [r10 + rsi], ymm7
          vmovups ymmword ptr [r10 + rsi + 32], ymm6
          vmovups ymmword ptr [r10 + rsi + 2048], ymm5
          vmovups ymmword ptr [r10 + rsi + 2080], ymm4
          vmovups ymmword ptr [r10 + rsi + 4096], ymm3
          vmovups ymmword ptr [r10 + rsi + 4128], ymm2
          vmovups ymmword ptr [r10 + rsi + 6144], ymm1
          vmovups ymmword ptr [r10 + rsi + 6176], ymm0
          inc
                  r9
          add     r8, 64
          cmp     r9, 32
          jne     .LBB2_2
          inc
                  rcx
          add     rax, 8192
          cmp     rcx, 128
          jne     .LBB2_1
          pop
                  rbx
          vzeroupper
          ret

The inner loop .LBB2_3 is the whole story. Read it line by line:

  • vmovups ymm8, [rbx - 32] and vmovups ymm9, [rbx]: load 16 floats of row k of B (2 registers of 8).
  • vbroadcastss ymm10, [rax + 4*r11 - 4096]: load one float of A and copy it into all 8 lanes. This happens 4 times, once per row of the tile. The offsets -4096, -2048, 0 and +2048 are 2048 bytes apart, which is exactly one row of A (512 floats × 4 bytes), measured from a base address the compiler chose.
  • 8 vfmadd231ps into ymm0 to ymm7: the 4 × 16 tile of C, held in 8 registers of 8 floats.
  • add rbx, 2048: move to the next row of B.

Per iteration: 6 loads, 8 FMAs = 128 FLOPs. And the 8 FMAs write 8 different accumulators, so there are 8 independent chains: enough to cover the FMA latency. Memory traffic per FLOP dropped from 3 memory ops per 16 FLOPs to 6 per 128.

The C code does not mention registers at all. It only arranged the loops so that a small block of results is reused, and the compiler did the register allocation. This is what an ML compiler’s “upcast” step produces: the compiler emits C code shaped like mm_tile, and checking the assembly for 8 independent vfmadd231ps with no loads or stores of the accumulators is how you know it worked.

What is still missing

68 GFLOP/s is good for one core and very simple code, but it is not the end. What fast libraries (OpenBLAS, MKL, oneDNN) add on top:

  • Cache blocking: split k and j into blocks so the slice of B being reused stays in L1 or L2, instead of streaming all of B from memory for every tile of rows.
  • Packing: copy blocks of A and B into a contiguous, exactly-ordered buffer first, so the inner kernel reads memory purely sequentially.
  • Bigger tiles: with AVX-512 there are 32 registers of 16 floats, so tiles like 6 × 32 or 14 × 32.
  • Threads: split the output across all cores.

Each of these is a loop transformation, not new math, which is why compilers can learn to produce them automatically.

Exercises

  1. How many floats of B does mm_tile load from memory in total for the whole multiply? Compare with mm_ikj.
  2. In the tile kernel, why 4 × 16 and not 16 × 16? (Count registers: there are 16 ymm registers.)
  3. Compile mm_tile with gcc instead of clang, and with -march=x86-64 (no AVX). What changes in the inner loop?
  4. Change the tile to 6 × 16. Does it still fit in registers? Predict the speed, then measure it.

title: How a GPU runs code
html:
A CPU core is built to finish one stream of instructions as fast as possible: big caches, out-of-order execution, branch prediction. A GPU is built for a different job: run the same small program on millions of data elements, and maximize total throughput even if each element takes a long time. Everything about GPU assembly follows from this. This chapter uses NVIDIA terms, since PTX and SASS are NVIDIA’s. AMD’s GPUs are organized the same way with different names.

The hardware

A GPU is made of many streaming multiprocessors (SMs). An A100 has 108 of them, an H100 (sxm) has 132. Each SM is a processor of its own with:

  • A large register file: 65,536 registers of 32 bits per SM (256 KB). Far bigger than a CPU core’s.
  • Several warp schedulers (4 per SM on recent chips), each able to issue one instruction per cycle.
  • Arithmetic units: many 32-bit float/int lanes, plus tensor cores for small matrix multiplies.
  • Shared memory: fast on-chip memory managed by the program, up to 164 KB per SM on A100 and 228 KB on H100 (it shares space with the L1 cache).

All SMs share an L2 cache (40 MB on A100, 50 MB on H100) and the big off-chip global memory (HBM), with bandwidth around 1.6 to 2 TB/s on A100 and about 3.35 TB/s on H100 sxm, but a latency of several hundred cycles per access.

Threads, warps, blocks, grids

You write a kernel: a function that one thread runs. You launch it with a grid of threads. The threads are organized in two levels:

  • A block is a group of up to 1024 threads. A block runs entirely on one SM. Its threads can share data through shared memory and wait for each other with a barrier.
  • The grid is all the blocks of one launch. Blocks run in any order, on any SM, and cannot wait for each other inside a kernel.

And one level the hardware adds by itself:

  • A warp is 32 consecutive threads of a block. The warp is the real unit of execution. The scheduler issues one instruction for a whole warp, and all 32 threads execute it at once, each on its own data. This is SIMD from chapter 10, with 32 lanes, except that each lane looks like a separate thread to the programmer. NVIDIA calls this SIMT.

Each thread knows where it is through built-in values: threadIdx.x (its index inside the block), blockIdx.x (its block’s index in the grid), blockDim.x (threads per block). The global index of a thread is almost always computed as:

i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x

And the simplest kernel uses it to pick which element to work on:

__global__ void vadd(const float *a, const float *b, float *c, int n) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i < n) c[i] = a[i] + b[i];
}

There is no loop. The loop over i is the grid itself: launch enough threads and each one handles one i. The if (i < n) handles the last block, which may have more threads than elements left.

Divergence

All 32 threads of a warp execute the same instruction. So what happens at if (x > 0) A else B when some threads have x > 0 and others do not? The warp runs both paths, one after the other, with the threads that should not participate switched off (masked). This is divergence. A branch where all 32 threads agree costs nothing extra. A branch where they disagree costs the sum of both sides. In assembly, you will see branches controlled by predicates: per-thread true/false registers that switch individual threads on or off.

Latency hiding: the core idea of GPUs

A global memory load takes hundreds of cycles. A CPU hides this with caches and out-of-order execution. A GPU mostly does not. Instead, each SM keeps many warps resident at once (up to 64 warps = 2048 threads on A100) and every cycle each scheduler picks some warp that is ready to run. While warp 3 waits for its load, warps 4, 5 and 6 compute. Switching warps costs nothing, because every warp’s registers stay in the register file the whole time.

This gives the main trade-off of GPU programming. Occupancy is how many warps an SM holds compared with its maximum. It is limited by resources:

  • Registers: 65,536 per SM. If a kernel uses 64 registers per thread, an SM can hold 65536 / 64 = 1024 threads = 32 warps. At 128 registers per thread, only 16 warps. At 255 (the maximum), about 8.
  • Shared memory: if each block uses 48 KB, at most 3 blocks fit in 164 KB.
  • Threads per block and blocks per SM limits.

More warps hide more latency. But more registers per thread allow bigger register tiles (chapter 12), which cut memory traffic. Fast kernels balance these two, and you see the balance in the assembly as the register count.

The memory spaces

SpaceWhereWho sees itSpeed
RegistersIn the SMOne threadFastest
Shared memoryIn the SMAll threads of one
block		About as fast as L1
Local memoryGlobal memoryOne threadSlow. Used when
(cached)registers run out
(spills)
Global memoryOff-chip HBMEveryoneHundreds of cycles,
but huge bandwidth
Constant memoryGlobal, with a specialEveryone, read-onlyFast when all threads
cacheread the same address

Coalescing

Global memory is read in 32-byte sectors. When the 32 threads of a warp each load a 4-byte float, the hardware merges their requests:

  • Thread t reads address base + 4t: all 32 addresses fall in 128 consecutive bytes, so 4 sectors serve the whole warp. This is coalesced access, and it is what vadd does.
  • Thread t reads address base + 4 * 512 * t (a column of a row-major matrix): 32 different sectors, each used for 4 of its 32 bytes. 8x more memory traffic for the same data.

On a GPU, consecutive threads should touch consecutive addresses. That rule decides which matrix dimension you map to threadIdx.x, and it is the GPU version of “walk arrays in order” from chapter 11.

From CUDA to machine code

kernel.cu --(nvcc / clang)--> ptx --(ptxas)--> sass, inside a .cubin file
  cuda c++                     virtual isa       the real machine code

PTX is a virtual instruction set: stable across GPU generations, with unlimited registers. SASS is the real machine code of one specific GPU generation, produced from PTX by the ptxas assembler, which does register allocation and instruction scheduling. A program can ship PTX and let the driver compile it for whatever GPU it lands on. The next two chapters read both.

Exercises

  1. A kernel is launched with 4096 blocks of 256 threads. How many threads in total? How many warps per block?
  2. A kernel uses 96 registers per thread. How many warps can one A100 SM hold, considering registers only?
  3. A warp executes if (threadIdx.x % 2 == 0) A(); else B();. How long does it take compared with only A?
  4. A 1024 × 1024 row-major float matrix is processed by a kernel where threadIdx.x picks the row and the thread loops over columns. Is the access coalesced? How would you fix it?

title: PTX
html:
PTX is the assembly language that CUDA compiles to first. It looks like a risc instruction set with types attached, and with unlimited registers. You read it to see what the compiler understood from your kernel: which loads it made, which memory space it used, whether it used vector loads, predicates, shuffles or tensor core instructions. Every listing in this chapter is real output of clang’s nvptx backend for sm_80 (A100), from the CUDA source shown above it.

The shape of a PTX instruction

opcode.modifier.type   destination, source1, source2;
  • add.f32 %f3, %f1, %f2; adds two f32 registers.
  • ld.global.f32 %f1, [%rd3]; loads an f32 from global memory at the address in %rd3.
  • mad.lo.s32 %r5, %r2, %r3, %r4; multiplies two signed 32-bit values, keeps the low 32 bits of the product, and adds a third.
  • setp.ge.s32 %p1, %r5, %r1; sets the predicate %p1 to (r5 >= r1).
  • @%p1 bra $L__BB0_2; branches only in threads where %p1 is true.

Types: .s32 / .u32 / .s64 / .u64 (signed and unsigned integers), .f16, .f32, .f64, .b32 / .b64 (raw bits), .pred (a true/false predicate).

Registers are virtual and declared in bulk at the top of each function, for example .reg .f32 %f<4>; declares %f0 to %f3. The names are a convention of the compiler: %r for 32-bit integers, %rd for 64-bit, %f for floats, %p for predicates. PTX does not care how many you use. ptxas maps them to real registers later.

Special registers

PTXCUDAMeaning

State spaces

Every load and store names the memory it touches:

Seeing ld.local or st.local in a kernel you expected to be fast is a warning sign. It means something did not fit in registers.

Vector add, line by line

extern "C" __global__ void vadd(const float *a, const float *b, float *c, int n) {int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i < n) c[i] = a[i] + b[i];
}
compiler output: clang, nvptx, sm_80

  .visible .entry vadd(
          .param .u64 vadd_param_0,
          .param .u64 vadd_param_1,
          .param .u64 vadd_param_2,
          .param .u32 vadd_param_3
  )
  {
          .reg .pred      %p<2>;
          .reg .b32       %r<6>;
          .reg .f32       %f<4>;
          .reg .b64       %rd<11>;
          ld.param.u32    %r1, [vadd_param_3];
          mov.u32         %r2, %ctaid.x;
          mov.u32         %r3, %ntid.x;
          mov.u32         %r4, %tid.x;
          mad.lo.s32      %r5, %r2, %r3, %r4;
          setp.ge.s32     %p1, %r5, %r1;
          @%p1 bra        $L__BB0_2;
          ld.param.u64    %rd4, [vadd_param_0];
          ld.param.u64    %rd5, [vadd_param_2];
          cvta.to.global.u64      %rd6, %rd5;
          ld.param.u64    %rd7, [vadd_param_1];
          cvta.to.global.u64      %rd8, %rd7;
          cvta.to.global.u64      %rd9, %rd4;
          mul.wide.s32    %rd10, %r5, 4;
          add.s64         %rd1, %rd6, %rd10;
          add.s64         %rd2, %rd8, %rd10;
          add.s64         %rd3, %rd9, %rd10;
          ld.global.f32   %f1, [%rd3];
          ld.global.f32   %f2, [%rd2];
          add.f32         %f3, %f1, %f2;
          st.global.f32   [%rd1], %f3;
  $L__BB0_2:
          ret;
  }
  1. The .entry header declares a kernel with four .param arguments: three 64-bit pointers and one 32-bit int.
  2. ld.param.u32 %r1, [vadd_param_3] loads n.
  3. Three mov s read %ctaid.x, %ntid.x, %tid.x, and mad.lo.s32 computes i = blockIdx × blockDim + threadIdx in one instruction.
  4. setp.ge.s32 sets %p1 = (i >= n), and @%p1 bra sends those threads to the end. This is the if.
  5. The pointer parameters are loaded and cvta.to.global converts each from a generic address to a global-space address.
  6. mul.wide.s32 %rd10, %r5, 4 multiplies the 32-bit i by 4 into a 64-bit result: the byte offset. (“wide” means the result is twice the width of the inputs.) then three add.s64 make the three addresses.
  7. Two ld.global.f32, one add.f32, one st.global.f32. The actual work is these four instructions. Everything before is index arithmetic.

That ratio is normal for small kernels: most instructions compute addresses. On a GPU this is cheap because the integer units run in parallel with memory traffic. The kernel’s speed is set by the two loads and one store, and since consecutive threads touch consecutive floats, they are coalesced.

Restrict and the read-only path

Mark the input pointers const float *__restrict__ and the loads become ld.global.nc.f32. .nc means “non-coherent”: the compiler has promised the data will not change during the kernel, so the hardware may serve it through the read-only texture/l1 path. You can see this in the reduction and matmul listings below.

Wider loads

A thread can load 16 bytes at once if the address is 16-byte aligned. This kernel processes 4 floats per thread through a 16-byte aligned struct:

struct __attribute__((aligned(16))) f4 { float x, y, z, w; };
extern "C" __global__ void vadd4(const f4 *__restrict__ a, const f4 *__restrict__ b,f4 *__restrict__ c, int n4) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i < n4) {
        f4 p = a[i], q = b[i];
        c[i] = f4{p.x + q.x, p.y + q.y, p.z + q.z, p.w + q.w};
    }
}

The memory instructions of the output:

compiler output: clang, nvptx, sm_80

  ld.global.nc.v4.f32     {%f1, %f2, %f3, %f4}, [%rd8];
  ld.global.nc.v4.f32     {%f5, %f6, %f7, %f8}, [%rd9];
  add.f32         %f9, %f1, %f5;
  add.f32         %f10, %f2, %f6;
  add.f32         %f11, %f3, %f7;
  add.f32         %f12, %f4, %f8;
  st.global.v4.f32        [%rd10], {%f9, %f10, %f11, %f12};

ld.global.nc.v4.f32 loads four floats into four registers with one instruction. Fewer, wider memory instructions mean fewer instructions issued per byte, which matters for memory-bound kernels. In CUDA this is what float4 does. In a compiler you generate it by grouping 4 consecutive elements per thread and proving alignment, which is the GPU form of upcasting.

A block reduction with shared memory

Summing 256 numbers per block: each thread writes its number into shared memory, then the block repeatedly halves the active threads, each adding a partner’s value, with a barrier between steps:

extern "C" __global__ void block_sum(const float *__restrict__ x, float *out, intn) {
    __shared__ float buf[256];
    int t = threadIdx.x;
    int i = blockIdx.x * 256 + t;
    buf[t] = i < n ? x[i] : 0.0f;
    __syncthreads();
    for (int s = 128; s > 0; s >>= 1) {
        if (t < s) buf[t] += buf[t + s];
        __syncthreads();
    }
    if (t == 0) out[blockIdx.x] = buf[0];
}

Compiled with loop unrolling off, so the loop is visible:

compiler output: clang, nvptx, sm_80

  .visible .entry block_sum(
          .param .u64 block_sum_param_0,
          .param .u64 block_sum_param_1,
          .param .u32 block_sum_param_2
  )
  {
          .reg .pred      %p<5>;
          .reg .b32       %r<10>;
          .reg .f32       %f<9>;
          .reg .b64       %rd<14>;
          // demoted variable
          .shared .align 4 .b8 _ZZ9block_sumE3buf[1024];
          ld.param.u64    %rd7, [block_sum_param_1];
          ld.param.u32    %r5, [block_sum_param_2];
          mov.u32         %r1, %tid.x;
          mov.u32         %r2, %ctaid.x;
          shl.b32         %r6, %r2, 8;
          add.s32         %r7, %r6, %r1;
          setp.ge.s32     %p1, %r7, %r5;
          mov.f32         %f8, 0f00000000;
          @%p1 bra        $L__BB0_2;
          ld.param.u64    %rd6, [block_sum_param_0];
          cvta.to.global.u64      %rd8, %rd6;
          mul.wide.s32    %rd9, %r7, 4;
          add.s64         %rd2, %rd8, %rd9;
          ld.global.nc.f32        %f8, [%rd2];
  $L__BB0_2:
          cvta.to.global.u64      %rd1, %rd7;
          mul.wide.s32    %rd10, %r1, 4;
          mov.u64         %rd11, _ZZ9block_sumE3buf;
          add.s64         %rd3, %rd11, %rd10;
          st.shared.f32   [%rd3], %f8;
          bar.sync        0;
          mov.b32         %r9, 128;
          bra.uni         $L__BB0_3;
  $L__BB0_5:
          bar.sync        0;
          shr.u32         %r4, %r9, 1;
          setp.lt.u32     %p3, %r9, 2;
          mov.u32         %r9, %r4;
          @%p3 bra        $L__BB0_6;
  $L__BB0_3:
          .pragma "nounroll";
          setp.ge.s32     %p2, %r1, %r9;
          @%p2 bra        $L__BB0_5;
          mul.wide.s32    %rd12, %r9, 4;
          add.s64         %rd5, %rd3, %rd12;
          ld.shared.f32   %f4, [%rd5];
          ld.shared.f32   %f5, [%rd3];
          add.f32         %f6, %f4, %f5;
          st.shared.f32   [%rd3], %f6;
          bra.uni         $L__BB0_5;
  $L__BB0_6:
          setp.eq.s32     %p4, %r1, 0;
          @%p4 bra        $L__BB0_7;
          bra.uni         $L__BB0_8;
  $L__BB0_7:
          mul.wide.u32    %rd13, %r2, 4;
          add.s64         %rd4, %rd1, %rd13;
          ld.shared.f32   %f7, [_ZZ9block_sumE3buf];
          st.global.f32   [%rd4], %f7;
  $L__BB0_8:
          ret;
  }

What to notice:

  • .shared .align 4 .b8 _ZZ9block_sumE3buf[1024]: the 256-float shared array, as 1024 raw bytes. (“demoted variable” means the compiler moved a variable declared inside the function into the shared state space, where it really lives.)
  • blockIdx.x * 256 became shl.b32 %r6, %r2, 8: shift left by 8.
  • The ternary i < n ? x[i] : 0.0f became: put 0 in %f8, and skip the load in threads where i >= n.
  • st.shared.f32 writes the thread’s value, and bar.sync 0 is __syncthreads(): every thread of the block waits there until all have arrived.
  • The loop ($L__BB0_3 and $L__BB0_5): threads with t >= s skip the add, but all threads reach the bar.sync. The shr.u32 halves s. It is a correctness rule that every thread of the block reaches every bar.sync. A barrier inside a branch that only some threads take can hang the GPU.
  • bra.uni is a branch the compiler knows all threads in the warp take the same way: a uniform branch, no divergence.

Bank conflicts: shared memory is split into 32 banks, each 4 bytes wide, with consecutive 4-byte words in consecutive banks. If the 32 threads of a warp access 32 different banks, it takes one cycle. If several threads access different addresses in the same bank, those accesses are serialized. Here thread t reads buf[t] and buf[t + s]: consecutive threads hit consecutive banks, so there are no conflicts. A column access in a 2d shared array with 32 columns would put every thread in the same bank, a 32-way conflict. The usual fix is to pad each row by one element.

Warp shuffles

Threads in a warp can read each other’s registers directly, without shared memory. shfl.sync.down gives each thread the value from the thread offset lanes higher. A warp-level sum:

extern "C" __global__ void warp_sum(const float *__restrict__ x, float *out) {
    float v = x[blockIdx.x * 32 + threadIdx.x];
    for (int off = 16; off > 0; off >>= 1)
        v += __nvvm_shfl_sync_down_f32(0xffffffff, v, off, 0x1f);
                                                                    //
__shfl_down_sync in cuda
    if (threadIdx.x == 0) out[blockIdx.x] = v;
}
compiler output: clang, nvptx, sm_80

  .visible .entry warp_sum(
          .param .u64 warp_sum_param_0,
          .param .u64 warp_sum_param_1
  )
  {
          .reg .pred      %p<2>;
          .reg .b32       %r<5>;
          .reg .f32       %f<12>;
          .reg .b64       %rd<9>;
          ld.param.u64    %rd2, [warp_sum_param_0];
          cvta.to.global.u64      %rd5, %rd2;
          mov.u32         %r1, %ctaid.x;
          shl.b32         %r2, %r1, 5;
          mov.u32         %r3, %tid.x;
          add.s32         %r4, %r2, %r3;
          mul.wide.u32    %rd6, %r4, 4;
          add.s64         %rd7, %rd5, %rd6;
          ld.global.nc.f32        %f2, [%rd7];
          shfl.sync.down.b32      %f3, %f2, 16, 31, -1;
          add.f32         %f4, %f2, %f3;
          shfl.sync.down.b32      %f5, %f4, 8, 31, -1;

          add.f32         %f1, %f10, %f11;

The compiler fully unrolled the loop into five shfl.sync.down.b32 and five add.f32: offsets 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. After the five steps, lane 0 holds the sum of all 32 values. The operands are: destination, source value, offset, a clamp value (31) and the member mask (-1 = all 32 lanes participate). No shared memory, no barrier. Fast reductions use shuffles inside each warp and shared memory only to combine warps.

Naive matrix multiply, and why it is slow

extern "C" __global__ void matmul(const float *__restrict__ A, const float *__restrict__ B,
                                  float *__restrict__ C, int M, int N, int K) {
    int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;
    int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (row >= M || col >= N) return;
    float acc = 0.0f;
    for (int k = 0; k < K; k++)
        acc += A[row * K + k] * B[k * N + col];
    C[row * N + col] = acc;
}

          .param .u64 matmul_param_0,
          .param .u64 matmul_param_1,
          .param .u64 matmul_param_2,
          .param .u32 matmul_param_3,
          .param .u32 matmul_param_4,
          .param .u32 matmul_param_5
  )
  {
          .reg .pred      %p<6>;
          .reg .b32       %r<20>;
          .reg .f32       %f<10>;
          .reg .b64       %rd<16>;
          ld.param.u32    %r7, [matmul_param_4];
          ld.param.u32    %r9, [matmul_param_3];
          mov.u32         %r10, %ctaid.y;
          mov.u32         %r11, %ntid.y;
          mov.u32         %r12, %tid.y;
          mad.lo.s32      %r1, %r10, %r11, %r12;
          mov.u32         %r13, %ctaid.x;

          ld.param.u32    %r19, [matmul_param_5];
          ld.param.u64    %rd8, [matmul_param_2];
          cvta.to.global.u64      %rd1, %rd8;
          setp.lt.s32     %p4, %r19, 1;
          mov.f32         %f9, 0f00000000;
          @%p4 bra        $L__BB0_4;
          ld.param.u64    %rd7, [matmul_param_0];
          ld.param.u64    %rd9, [matmul_param_1];
          cvta.to.global.u64      %rd2, %rd9;
          cvta.to.global.u64      %rd3, %rd7;
          mul.lo.s32      %r16, %r1, %r19;
          mul.wide.s32    %rd10, %r16, 4;
          add.s64         %rd15, %rd3, %rd10;
          mov.f32         %f9, 0f00000000;
          mov.u32         %r18, %r2;
  $L__BB0_3:
          .pragma "nounroll";
          ld.global.nc.f32        %f6, [%rd15];
          mul.wide.s32    %rd11, %r18, 4;
          add.s64         %rd12, %rd2, %rd11;
          ld.global.nc.f32        %f7, [%rd12];
          fma.rn.f32      %f9, %f6, %f7, %f9;
          add.s32         %r19, %r19, -1;
          add.s32         %r18, %r18, %r7;
          add.s64         %rd15, %rd15, 4;
          setp.eq.s32     %p5, %r19, 0;
          @%p5 bra        $L__BB0_4;
          bra.uni         $L__BB0_3;
  $L__BB0_4:
          mad.lo.s32      %r17, %r1, %r7, %r2;
          mul.wide.s32    %rd13, %r17, 4;
          add.s64         %rd14, %rd1, %rd13;
          st.global.f32   [%rd14], %f9;
  $L__BB0_5:
          ret;
  }

The inner loop is $L__BB0_3. Per iteration: two ld.global.nc.f32, one fma.rn.f32 (fused multiply-add, round to nearest), and loop bookkeeping. Two global loads for every 2 FLOPs. This is the GPU version of the textbook matmul from chapter 12, and it is memory bound for the same reason.

The access pattern is not all bad. col comes from threadIdx.x, so the 32 threads of a warp read 32 consecutive floats of B: coalesced. All 32 threads read the same A element: one sector, broadcast to all. The real problem is reuse: each value is loaded from global memory once per thread that needs it, with no sharing.

The standard fix has two levels, exactly mirroring the CPU:

  1. Shared memory tiling: a block loads a tile of A and a tile of B into shared memory once (ld.global then st.shared, then bar.sync), and all its threads read the tiles from there many times (ld.shared).
  2. Register tiling: each thread computes a small block of C (say 8 × 8) in registers, so each value it reads from shared memory is used 8 times.

In the PTX of a well-tiled kernel, the inner loop is mostly fma.rn.f32 with a few ld.shared (often .v4) between them, and ld.global only in the outer loop.

Tensor cores

Tensor cores multiply small matrices in one instruction per warp. The PTX is:

mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k16.row.col.f32.f16.f16.f32  {d0,d1,d2,d3}, {a0,a1,a2,a3},{b0,b1}, {c0,c1,c2,c3};

Reading the name: a warp-wide (sync, aligned) matrix multiply-accumulate with shape m16 n8 k16: a 16 × 16 tile of A times a 16 × 8 tile of B, added to a 16 × 8 tile of C. A is row-major, B column-major. The output and accumulator are f32, the inputs f16. Each of the 32 threads holds a few fragments of each matrix in its registers, in a layout fixed by the PTX documentation. ldmatrix loads those fragments from shared memory in the right layout. On Hopper (H100), the newer wgmma instructions work on a group of 4 warps and read operands straight from shared memory.

When you check whether a kernel uses tensor cores, you look for mma in the PTX or HMMA in the SASS. If they are not there, the kernel is running on the normal FMA units at a fraction of the GPU’s possible throughput.

Writing PTX by hand: inline assembly

You rarely write whole kernels in PTX, but you do drop single instructions into CUDA when there is no C++ way to express them. The syntax is the same as gcc inline assembly:

extern "C" __global__ void lane_ids(unsigned *out) {
    unsigned lane;
    asm volatile("mov.u32 %0, %%laneid;" : "=r"(lane));
    out[blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x] = lane;
}

%0 refers to the first operand, "=r"(lane) says it is an output in a 32-bit register bound to lane, and %% writes a literal %. The instruction lands verbatim in the output:

compiler output: clang, nvptx, sm_80

  {
          .reg .b32       %r<6>;
          .reg .b64       %rd<5>;
          ld.param.u64    %rd1, [lane_ids_param_0];
          cvta.to.global.u64      %rd2, %rd1;
          mov.u32 %r1, %laneid;
          mov.u32         %r2, %ctaid.x;
          mov.u32         %r3, %ntid.x;
          mov.u32         %r4, %tid.x;
          mad.lo.s32      %r5, %r2, %r3, %r4;
          mul.wide.u32    %rd3, %r5, 4;
          add.s64         %rd4, %rd2, %rd3;
          st.global.u32   [%rd4], %r1;
          ret;
  }

The same mechanism is used for cp.async (asynchronous copies from global to shared memory), special cache hints, and mma in hand-tuned kernels.

Exercises

  1. In the vadd PTX, which instructions would disappear if n were known to be a multiple of the block size and the if were removed?
  2. Why does block_sum need a bar.sync inside the loop, and not just one at the end?
  3. A 32 × 32 float array in shared memory is read column-wise by a warp (thread t reads tile[t][c]). Which bank does each thread hit? What does declaring it as tile[32][33] change?
  4. In the naive matmul, how many bytes of global memory traffic does one thread cause for K = 1024? How many FLOPs does it do?
  5. Compile vadd yourself with nvcc -ptx or on godbolt with nvcc. Compare with the clang output here. What differs?

title: SASS
html:
SASS is the machine code the GPU actually executes. ptxas produces it from PTX: it assigns real registers, picks real instructions, and schedules them. SASS changes with every GPU generation (Volta is sm_70, Ampere A100 is sm_80, Hopper H100 is sm_90), and NVIDIA does not publish a complete specification. You read it anyway, because it is the only place you can see the final register count, spills, the real memory instructions, and whether tensor cores are used.

Getting SASS

nvcc -cubin -arch=sm_80 kernel.cu -o kernel.cubin
cuobjdump -sass kernel.cubin

nvdisasm gives a lower-level view of the same file. Nsight compute’s “source” page shows SASS side by side with your CUDA code and with per-instruction stall statistics, which is the most useful view of all. The CUDA toolkit installs and runs on a machine without a GPU, so you can study SASS on a laptop.

The vector add in SASS

A note on this listing: the environment where this book was built had no NVIDIA toolchain, so unlike every other listing in this book, this one was not printed by a tool during the build. It shows the standard shape of what nvcc (CUDA 12) produces for the vadd kernel on sm_80. Register numbers and the order of independent instructions may differ in your output. The instructions and their meaning will not.

MOV R1, c[0x0][0x28]                            // set up the stack pointer (unusedhere)
S2R R6, SR_CTAID.X                              // R6 = blockIdx.x
S2R R3, SR_TID.X                                // R3 = threadIdx.x
IMAD R6, R6, c[0x0][0x0], R3                    // R6 = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x +threadIdx.x = i
ISETP.GE.AND P0, PT, R6, c[0x0][0x178], PT      // P0 = (i >= n)
@P0 EXIT                                        // threads with i >= n stop here
HFMA2.MMA R7, -RZ, RZ, 0, 2.384185791015625e-07 // R7 = 4 (see below)
ULDC.64 UR4, c[0x0][0x118]                      // memory descriptor into a uniformregister
IMAD.WIDE R4, R6, R7, c[0x0][0x168]             // R4:R5 = b + i * 4
IMAD.WIDE R2, R6, R7, c[0x0][0x160]             // R2:R3 = a + i * 4
LDG.E R4, desc[UR4][R4.64]                      // R4 = b[i]
LDG.E R3, desc[UR4][R2.64]                      // R3 = a[i]
IMAD.WIDE R6, R6, R7, c[0x0][0x170]             // R6:R7 = c + i * 4
FADD R9, R4, R3                                 // R9 = a[i] + b[i]
STG.E desc[UR4][R6.64], R9                      // c[i] = R9
EXIT
BRA 0x...                                       // padding: a jump to itself, neverreached

Reading it

Registers. R0 to R254 are 32-bit per-thread registers. RZ always reads as zero (like RISC- V’s x0). A 64-bit value uses a pair: R2.64 means R2 (low half) with R3 (high half). P0 to P6 are predicate registers, PT always reads as true. UR registers are uniform registers (Turing and later): one value for the whole warp, used for things every thread agrees on, like the memory descriptor here.

Constant bank 0. c[0x0][offset] reads from constant memory bank 0, where the driver puts launch information. c[0x0][0x0] is blockDim.x. On sm_70 and sm_80 the kernel parameters start at offset 0x160: so a is at 0x160, b at 0x168, c at 0x170 (each 8 bytes) and n at 0x178. Reading a parameter costs nothing extra, because most instructions can take a constant-bank operand directly. On sm_90 the parameters start at a different offset (0x210).

Special registers. S2R (“special to register”) reads SR_TID.X, SR_CTAID.X and similar. It has a long latency, so the compiler issues these first.

Predication. ISETP.GE.AND P0, PT, R6, c[0x0][0x178], PT is an integer compare that writes P0. The two PT operands are an extra predicate combined with AND, unused here. @P0 EXIT runs EXIT only in threads where P0 is true. Any instruction can be predicated this way, which is how short if s compile without branches.

IMAD.WIDE. A 32 × 32 bit multiply-add producing a 64-bit result in a register pair. IMAD.WIDE R2, R6, R7, c[0x0][0x160] computes a + i * 4 as a 64-bit address in one instruction. Note there is no separate “add the base pointer”: the base comes straight from the constant bank.

The 4 in R7. HFMA2.MMA R7, -RZ, RZ, 0, 2.384185791015625e-07 is a trick. HFMA2 does two half-precision FMAs on the two 16-bit halves of a register. Here it computes (-0 × 0) + k, which just writes the constant k. The constant’s bit pattern is 0x00000004: in the low half, 0x0004 read as an f16 is 2^-24 × 4 = 2.38e-07, and the high half is 0. So R7 gets the integer 4. The compiler uses this instead of a MOV because the .MMA form runs on a different execution unit, leaving the integer units free. You will see this odd-looking instruction all the time. It just loads a constant.

Memory. LDG.E is a load from global memory, .E meaning a 64-bit address. desc[UR4] attaches a memory descriptor (CUDA 11 and earlier print the same instruction without it). STG.E is the store. Other memory instructions you will meet:

ld.global.v4.f32 and similar)

(ld.global.nc)

LDG.E.CONSTANT

                                           __syncthreads()

SHFL.DOWN, SHFL.BFLY Warp shuffles

Arithmetic. FADD, FMUL, FFMA are f32 add, multiply, FMA. HFMA2 does 2 f16 FMAs at once. IADD3 adds three integers. LOP3 computes any logic function of three inputs, selected by an 8-bit lookup table. HMMA.16816.F32 is the tensor core instruction behind mma.m16n8k16 with f32 accumulation, and on Hopper HGMMA is behind wgmma.

What to look for

When you open the SASS of a kernel you care about, check these in order:

  1. The register count (printed by nvcc -Xptxas -v or shown in Nsight compute). It sets the occupancy (chapter 13).
  2. LDL and STL . Any spills in the hot loop are a serious problem. The fix is fewer live values (a smaller register tile) or an explicit register limit with __launch_bounds__.
  3. The width of memory instructions. LDG.E.128 and LDS.128 where you expected vectorized access. Plain LDG.E in a loop over many consecutive floats means the vector loads did not happen, usually because alignment could not be proven.
  4. The inner loop’s ratio of math to memory. A good matmul inner loop is a long run of FFMA or HMMA with a few LDS between them. A loop that is half LDG is memory bound.
  5. Tensor cores. For f16/bf16 matmuls, HMMA must be there. If it is not, the kernel uses a small fraction of the GPU’s possible throughput.
  6. BAR.SYNC count in the main loop. Each one makes the whole block wait.

Scheduling is in the instructions

On a CPU, the hardware decides at run time which instruction can go next (out-of-order execution). NVIDIA GPUs mostly do not: ptxas decides, and encodes control information inside each instruction: how many cycles to wait before issuing the next instruction, and which scoreboard barriers a slow operation (like a load) sets and which instructions wait on them. cuobjdump does not print these bits by default, but they are why the order of instructions in SASS matters and why ptxas spends so long on big kernels. It is also why the same PTX can produce kernels of quite different speed with different ptxas versions.

Exercises

  1. In the SASS above, which instructions correspond to the PTX mad.lo.s32 and setp.ge.s32 + @%p1 bra?
  2. Why does the vector add have only one EXIT for the “i >= n” threads and no branch?
  3. A kernel’s SASS shows STL [R1+0x10], R12 in its inner loop. What does it mean, and what would you try first?
  4. Compile vadd4 from chapter 14 for sm_80 and find the 128-bit loads in its SASS.

title: Assembly and ML compilers
html:
ML compilers like tinygrad, Triton and TVM take a graph of tensor operations and generate kernels from it. Many of them never emit assembly themselves: they generate C, CUDA or LLVM IR and let clang, nvcc or LLVM do the last step. This chapter uses a tinygrad-style design as its example, where the graph is made of small ops called uops and the output is C or CUDA. If you build or work on such a compiler, assembly is how you check that the generated code does what you meant, and how you find out why it is slow.

How uops become instructions

Every uop ends up as a recognizable pattern in the final machine code. Once you know the mapping, you can read a kernel’s assembly and point at the uop each instruction came from.

The most important line is RANGE. On a CPU a range is a loop and costs instructions every iteration. On a GPU, a range mapped to a thread axis costs nothing at run time: it becomes the thread’s own index. Deciding which ranges become loops and which become thread indices is most of what a GPU code generator does.

What to check as the compiler grows

Stage 1: correctness and simplification. Speed is not the goal yet, but assembly is still useful: compile your generated C with -O2 and look at it. If your symbolic simplifier left (x * 4 + 2) / 4 in the index math, the C compiler may or may not clean it up. If you see a division or a div7 -style magic multiply inside a hot loop, your index simplification missed a case. Clean index math in the C source should become a pointer that adds a constant each iteration.

Stage 2: fast CPU kernels. This is where reading assembly becomes the main tool. For a matmul or reduce kernel your compiler generated, check:

  1. The inner loop uses ps and ymm (or zmm) instructions, not ss and xmm. If not, it did not vectorize; find out why with -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize.
  2. Reductions are split across several independent accumulator registers. One accumulator means one dependency chain, which caps the loop at the FMA latency (chapter 11).
  3. Accumulators stay in registers for the whole k loop: no stores and reloads of them inside the loop.
  4. The ratio of loads to FMAs is low. The tile kernel of chapter 12 had 6 loads per 8 FMAs. A loop with more loads than FMAs is memory bound.
  5. There are no spills. On x86 a spill is a store to [rsp + ...] inside the hot loop followed by a reload.

Stage 3: GPU kernels. For each generated kernel, compile to PTX and SASS and check:

  1. Consecutive threads touch consecutive addresses (coalescing). Look at how %tid.x enters the address computation. It should be multiplied by the element size only, not by a row stride.
  2. Loads are as wide as they can be: ld.global.v4.f32, LDG.E.128.
  3. Shared memory tiles exist when data is reused: st.shared, bar.sync, then many ld.shared in the inner loop.
  4. No ld.local / st.local / LDL / STL.
  5. For matmuls in f16 or bf16: mma in PTX, HMMA in SASS.
  6. The register count leaves enough occupancy (chapter 13).

A checklist you can print

When someone hands you a slow kernel, go through this in order, and stop at the first thing that is wrong:

  1. Is it computing what you think? (Read the inner loop and map every instruction to the source.)
  2. Is it memory bound or compute bound? (Count bytes and FLOPs; compare with the roofline.)
  3. If memory bound: is the access in order and coalesced, are loads wide, is data reused from registers or shared memory instead of reloaded?
  4. If compute bound: is it vectorized or on tensor cores, are there enough independent accumulators, is anything a division or a branch that could be removed?
  5. Is anything spilling?
  6. Only then: measure with perf or Nsight compute, change one thing, measure again.

Most of the time, the problem is found at step 3.

Where to go next

  • Read the assembly of real kernels: the SASS of a CUTLASS or flash-attention kernel in Nsight compute, and the generated C and PTX of tinygrad (DEBUG=4 prints generated code).
  • The RISC-V specification volume 1 is short and readable. The Intel software developer’s manual volume 2 is the x86 reference. The PTX ISA document from NVIDIA is the PTX reference and is very good.
  • uops.info for x86 instruction costs. Agner fog’s optimization manuals for how x86 cores work inside.
  • “computer systems: a programmer’s perspective” (Bryant and o’hallaron) for the full systems picture. “programming massively parallel processors” (Hwu, Kirk, El Hajj) for GPUs.

title: Exercise solutions
html:
Every code solution below was assembled and run: RISC-V in the emulator against a Python reference, x86-64 natively against a C test program. Where an exercise asks you to try something on godbolt, the answer says what you should find.

Chapter 1

  1. 0xb7 = 1011 0111 = 183 unsigned. Signed 8-bit: -128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 + 1 = -73.
  2. -1 is 0xffffffff. -2 is 0xfffffffe.
  3. lb: 0xffffffffffffff80 (the sign bit is copied up, the value is -128). lbu: 0x0000000000000080 (128).
  4. The bytes from address 0x1000 are ef be ad de, so 0x1001 holds 0xbe.
  5. -9 >> 3 is -2: the shift rounds toward negative infinity, so -1.125 becomes -2. -9 / 8 is -1, because C division rounds toward zero.

Chapter 3

  1. No multiply:
ex_lin.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # a0 = 3 * a0 + 7, no mul
      .globl lin
  lin:
      slli t0, a0, 1
                          # t0 = 2x
      add  a0, a0, t0     # a0 = x + 2x = 3x
      addi a0, a0, 7
                          # a0 = 3x + 7
      ret
  1. Two answers, both tested:
ex_sign.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # a0 = 1 if a0 < 0 else 0, two ways
      .globl is_neg1
  is_neg1:
      slt  a0, a0, zero   # compare with zero (signed)
      ret
      .globl is_neg2
  is_neg2:
      srli a0, a0, 63
                          # move the sign bit down to bit 0
      ret
  1. 2048 does not fit in a 12-bit signed immediate (the maximum is 2047), so it needs two instructions. LLVM emits li t0, 1 then slli t0, t0, 11. Another correct form is lui t0, 1 (4096) then addiw t0, t0, -2048.
  2. -1 is all ones. Shifting right logically by 60 leaves 4 ones: t0 = 15.

Chapter 4

  1. Max: the listing in chapter 5 (max.s).
  2. Rev: the listing in chapter 5 (rev.s). The beqz a1 at the top handles n = 0, where “the last element” would be one element before the array.
  3. Dot product:
ex_dot.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long dot(long *a, long *b, long n)
      .globl dot
  dot:
      li   t0, 0
                          # total
      slli a2, a2, 3
      add  a2, a0, a2     # end of a
  1:
      beq  a0, a2, 2f
      ld   t1, 0(a0)
      ld   t2, 0(a1)
      mul  t1, t1, t2
      add  t0, t0, t1
      addi a0, a0, 8
      addi a1, a1, 8
      j    1b
  2:
      mv   a0, t0
      ret
  1. val is at offset 0, next at offset 8:
ex_list.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # struct node { long val; struct node *next; };   val at 0, next at 8
  # long list_sum(struct node *p)
      .globl list_sum
  list_sum:
      li   t0, 0
  1:
      beqz a0, 2f         # null pointer ends the list
      ld   t1, 0(a0)
                          # p->val
      add  t0, t0, t1
      ld   a0, 8(a0)
                          # p = p->next
      j    1b
  2:
      mv   a0, t0
      ret
  1. blt compares addresses as signed numbers. On Linux user space, addresses are below 2^47, so they never look negative and it would work in practice. It is still wrong in principle: addresses are unsigned, so bltu is the correct comparison. beq / bne avoids the question entirely, which is why compilers use it.

Chapter 5

  1. Gcd:
ex_gcd.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long gcd(long a, long b): euclid, inputs >= 0
      .globl gcd
  gcd:
  1:
      beqz a1, 2f         # while (b != 0)
      rem  t0, a0, a1     #   t = a % b
      mv   a0, a1         #   a = b
      mv   a1, t0         #   b = t
      j    1b
  2:
      ret
  1. Binary search over [lo, hi):
ex_bsearch.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long bsearch(long *a, long n, long x): index of x in sorted a, or -1
      .globl bsearch
  bsearch:
      li   t0, 0
                          # lo = 0
      mv   t1, a1         # hi = n    (search range is [lo, hi))
  1:
      bge  t0, t1, 4f     # empty range: not found
      add  t2, t0, t1
      srli t2, t2, 1
                          # mid = (lo + hi) / 2
      slli t3, t2, 3
      add  t3, a0, t3
      ld   t3, 0(t3)
                          # t3 = a[mid]
      beq  t3, a2, 3f     # found
      blt  t3, a2, 2f     # a[mid] < x: go right
      mv   t1, t2         # else go left: hi = mid
      j    1b
  2:
      addi t0, t2, 1
                          # lo = mid + 1
      j    1b
  3:
      mv   a0, t2
      ret
  4:
      li   a0, -1
      ret
  1. Bubble sort:
ex_bubble.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # void bubble(long *a, long n): sort ascending
      .globl bubble
  bubble:
      addi a1, a1, -1
                          # outer: passes = n - 1
  1:
      blez a1, 4f         # no passes left
      mv   t0, a0         # p = a
      slli t1, a1, 3
      add  t1, a0, t1     # last = a + passes   (compare p[0] with p[1] while p <
  last)
  2:
      bgeu t0, t1, 3f
      ld   t2, 0(t0)
      ld   t3, 8(t0)
      ble  t2, t3, 5f     # already in order
      sd   t3, 0(t0)
                          # swap
      sd   t2, 8(t0)
  5:
      addi t0, t0, 8
      j    2b
  3:
      addi a1, a1, -1
                          # the biggest value is now at the end; one fewer pass
      j    1b
  4:
      ret
  1. Max with a rotated loop:
ex_max_rot.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long max(long *a, long n), n >= 1, rotated loop: one branch at the bottom
      .globl max_rot
  max_rot:
      ld   t0, 0(a0)
                          # best = a[0]
      slli a1, a1, 3
      add  a1, a0, a1     # end
      addi a0, a0, 8
                          # p = &a[1]
      beq  a0, a1, 3f     # n == 1: nothing else to look at
  1:
      ld   t1, 0(a0)
      bge  t0, t1, 2f
      mv   t0, t1
  2:
      addi a0, a0, 8
      bne  a0, a1, 1b     # test and jump back in one instruction
  3:
      mv   a0, t0
      ret
  1. With bgeu, x = -5 is read as an enormous unsigned number, so “x >= lo” is true and the function goes on to compare with hi. -5 compared unsigned with hi is again “greater”, so clamp returns hi instead of lo. A wrong answer from a single wrong letter.

Chapter 6

  1. square calls nothing, so nothing overwrites ra. sum_squares executes call square, which writes a new value into ra.
  2. T0 is caller-saved. The recursive call fib is allowed to overwrite t0 (and does, since fib itself uses t0). After the call, n would be garbage.
  3. Recursive sum:
ex_sumrec.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

  # long sum_rec(long *a, long n) = n == 0 ? 0 : a[0] + sum_rec(a + 1, n - 1)
      .globl sum_rec
  sum_rec:
      bnez a1, 1f
      li   a0, 0
                          # base case
      ret
  1:
      addi sp, sp, -16
      sd   ra, 8(sp)
      sd   s0, 0(sp)
      ld   s0, 0(a0)
                          # s0 = a[0], needed after the call
      addi a0, a0, 8
                          # a + 1
      addi a1, a1, -1
                          # n - 1
      call sum_rec
      add  a0, s0, a0     # a[0] + sum_rec(...)
      ld   s0, 0(sp)
      ld   ra, 8(sp)
      addi sp, sp, 16
      ret

For n = 2 there are two frames on the stack at the deepest point (from the calls with n = 2 and n = 1), each holding a saved ra and a saved s0. The n = 0 call returns without a frame.

  1. 5 registers × 8 bytes = 40 bytes, rounded up to 48 to keep sp a multiple of 16.
  2. After the callee returns, the caller would immediately return too, using the same ra. So the caller can restore its saved registers, free its frame, and jump straight to the callee, which will return directly to the caller’s caller. The caller’s frame is gone before the callee starts, so deep chains of tail calls use no extra stack.

Chapter 7

  1. Two writes (note that a0 must be set again, because the first ecall put its return value there):
ex_hello2.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

      .section .rodata
  m1: .ascii "first line\n"
      .set n1, . - m1
  m2: .ascii "second line\n"
      .set n2, . - m2
      .text
      .globl _start
  _start:
      li   a0, 1
      la   a1, m1
      li   a2, n1
      li   a7, 64
      ecall
      li   a0, 1
                          # a0 was overwritten by the first write's return value
      la   a1, m2
      li   a2, n2
      li   a7, 64
      ecall
      li   a0, 0
      li   a7, 93
      ecall
  1. Exit with status 42:
ex_exit42.s · risc-v, run and checked in an emulator

      .text
      .globl _start
  _start:
      li   a0, 42
                          # exit status
      li   a7, 93
                          # exit
      ecall
  1. Funct7 for sub is 0100000, which sets bit 30: 0x407302b3. The assembler agrees: bytes b3 02 73 40.
  2. The immediate is a signed 20-bit count of 2-byte units: up to (2^19 - 1) × 2 = 1,048,574 bytes forward, about 1 MB. That is why call sometimes becomes auipc + jalr, which can reach ±2 GB.

Chapter 8

  1. clang walks a pointer up to an end address, like ex_max_rot.s above. RV64IM has no conditional move instruction, so the update stays a branch (blt).
  2. x * 9 becomes lea rax, [rdi + 8*rdi]. x * 10 becomes add rdi, rdi (2x) followed by lea rax, [rdi + 4*rdi] (5 × 2x). No imul in either.
  3. The magic number is 3435973837 (0xcccccccd), followed by a shift right of 35: x / 10 == (x * 0xcccccccd) >> 35. For x = 1000: 3,435,973,837,000 / 2^35 = 100.000000005, which truncates to 100.
  4. The whole loop is gone. A function returning nothing compiles to a bare ret.

Chapter 9

  1. Rev in x86-64:
ex_rev.s · x86-64, run and checked natively

  # void rev(long *a, long n)
      .intel_syntax noprefix
      .globl rev
  rev:
      test rsi, rsi
      jz   .Ldone                         # n == 0
      lea  rax, [rdi + 8*rsi - 8]
                                          # rax = hi = &a[n-1];  rdi = lo
  .Lloop:
      cmp  rdi, rax
      jae  .Ldone                         # stop when lo >= hi (unsigned)
      mov  rcx, qword ptr [rdi]
      mov  rdx, qword ptr [rax]
      mov  qword ptr [rdi], rdx
      mov  qword ptr [rax], rcx
      add  rdi, 8
      sub
           rax, 8
      jmp  .Lloop
  .Ldone:
      ret
  1. mov eax, 5 zeroes the upper 32 bits: rax = 5. mov al, 5 changes only the low byte: rax = 0xffffffffffffff05. Both tested on real hardware.
  2. Dot product:
ex_dot.s · x86-64, run and checked natively

  # long dot(long *a, long *b, long n)      rdi = a, rsi = b, rdx = n
      .intel_syntax noprefix
      .globl dot
  dot:
      xor
           eax, eax
                                          # total
      xor
           ecx, ecx
                                          # i
  .Lloop:
      cmp  rcx, rdx
      jge  .Ldone
      mov  r8, qword ptr [rdi + 8*rcx]
      imul r8, qword ptr [rsi + 8*rcx]
                                          # r8 = a[i] * b[i]
      add  rax, r8
      inc
           rcx
      jmp  .Lloop
  .Ldone:
      ret
  1. A negative signed index, read as unsigned, is a number at least 2^63, far larger than any length. So the single unsigned test “index < length” rejects both negative and too-large indices.
  2. On entry rsp ends in 8. Two pushes move it by 16, so it still ends in 8: misaligned at the call. The function must also subtract 8 (or push a third register). With three pushes it ends in 0: aligned.

Chapter 10

  1. Without restrict, clang adds a run-time check that compares the two pointer ranges and keeps both a vector loop and a scalar loop, choosing at run time.
  2. Without -ffast-math: only scalar vaddss, one chain. With it: vaddps into four ymm accumulators (32 floats per iteration), combined at the end.
  3. N = 3 is below 4, so cmp rsi, 4 / jae is not taken: rcx and rax are zeroed and execution jumps straight to the scalar tail, which runs 3 times. The vector loop never runs.
  4. 16 lanes, each a multiply and an add: 32 FLOPs.

Chapter 11

  1. 1 million × 4 cycles = 4 million cycles = 1.33 ms at 3 GHz. With 8 chains and 2 adds started per cycle: 500,000 cycles = 0.17 ms.
  2. In pointer chasing, each load’s address comes from the previous load, so only one load is ever in flight: total time = count × latency. In-order access has independent addresses and a prefetcher, so many loads overlap and the limit becomes bytes per second.
  3. A dot product loads 8 bytes per element and does 2 FLOPs: 0.25 FLOPs per byte. At 16 GB/s that is 4 GFLOP/s: memory bound.
  4. About half the branches go each way at random, so roughly 0.5 mispredictions per element. perf will report close to that.

Chapter 12

  1. Each 4 × 16 tile reads 16 floats of B for each of 512 values of k. There are 128 × 32 = 4096 tiles: 4096 × 512 × 16 = 33.5 million floats. mm_ikj reads all of B (262,144 floats) for each of 512 rows of A: 134 million floats. The tile version reads 4x less B.
  2. 16 × 16 would need 32 accumulator registers of 8 floats, plus registers for the loaded B values and the broadcast A. There are only 16 ymm registers. 4 × 16 needs 8 accumulators + 2 + 1 = 11.
  3. gcc may not fully unroll the inner ii / jj loops, leaving accumulators in memory. Without AVX, only xmm registers (4 floats) and no FMA are available.
  4. 6 × 16 needs 12 accumulators + 2 + 1 = 15 registers: it fits. It reuses each B load 6 times instead of 4, so it should be somewhat faster. Measure it.

Chapter 13

  1. 4096 × 256 = 1,048,576 threads. 256 / 32 = 8 warps per block.
  2. 96 registers × 32 threads = 3072 registers per warp. 65536 / 3072 = 21 warps.
  3. Both paths run one after the other with half the threads masked: about the time of A plus B.
  4. No. At each step, the 32 threads of a warp read 32 different rows, 4096 bytes apart: 32 sectors per load. Map the column index to threadIdx.x instead, so a warp reads 32 consecutive floats of one row.

Chapter 14

  1. The setp.ge.s32 and the @%p1 bra, and the load of n.
  2. In each step, threads read values that other threads wrote in the previous step. Without a barrier, a thread could read a partner’s slot before the partner has finished writing it.
  3. Word tile[t][c] is at index 32*t + c, so its bank is (32*t + c) % 32 = c: every thread hits the same bank, a 32-way conflict. With 33 columns the index is 33*t + c and the bank is (t + c) % 32: all different banks.
  4. Per k: 2 loads of 4 bytes = 8 bytes. For K = 1024: 8 KB of loads, plus 4 bytes stored. 2 FLOPs per k: 2048 FLOPs. 0.25 FLOPs per byte.
  5. nvcc’s PTX uses different register names and usually computes the addresses in a slightly different order. The loads, the add and the store are the same.

Chapter 15

  1. IMAD R6, R6, c[0x0][0x0], R3 is the mad.lo.s32. ISETP.GE.AND plus @P0 EXIT replace setp.ge.s32 plus the predicated branch.
  2. After the bounds test there is nothing left for those threads to do, so the compiler makes them exit with a predicated EXIT instead of jumping to the end.
  3. A store to local memory at offset 0x10 from the per-thread stack pointer R1: a register spill. Reduce the number of live values in the loop (a smaller register tile, less unrolling) and check the register count with -Xptxas -v.
  4. Look for LDG.E.128 (and STG.E.128).

Compiling to assembly

clang -O2 -S file.c -o -                        # x86-64, at&t syntax
clang -O2 -S -masm=intel file.c -o -            # x86-64, intel syntax
clang -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 -S -masm=intel ...   # allow avx2 and fma
clang --target=riscv64 -march=rv64im -O2 -S file.c -o -
rustc -C opt-level=3 --emit=asm --crate-type=lib file.rs
cargo rustc --release -- --emit=asm             # for a cargo project

RISC-V on an x86 machine

sudo apt install gcc-riscv64-linux-gnu qemu-user
riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc -nostdlib -static prog.s -o prog && qemu-riscv64 ./prog
riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc -static test.c func.s -o test && qemu-riscv64 ./test

x86-64

gcc -nostdlib -static prog.s -o prog && ./prog    # a whole program with _start
gcc -O1 test.c func.s -o test && ./test           # functions called from c

Inspecting binaries

objdump -d -M intel prog        # disassemble
objdump -r file.o               # relocations
nm prog                         # symbols
llvm-mc -show-encoding f.s      # print the bytes of each instruction

Measuring

perf stat ./prog                            # cycles, instructions, ipc
perf stat -e branch-misses,cache-misses ./prog
perf record ./prog && perf report           # where time goes
perf annotate                               # hot instructions in the assembly
llvm-mca -mcpu=skylake loop.s               # static analysis of a loop

GPU

nvcc -ptx -arch=sm_80 k.cu                  # ptx
nvcc -cubin -arch=sm_80 k.cu -o k.cubin     # machine code
cuobjdump -sass k.cubin                     # sass
nvcc -Xptxas -v -arch=sm_80 -c k.cu         # register count, spills, shared memoryncu --set full ./prog                       # nsight compute profile

clang can also emit PTX without the CUDA toolkit, which is how this book’s PTX was made:

clang++ -x cuda --cuda-gpu-arch=sm_80 --cuda-device-only -nocudainc -nocudalib -O2 -S k.cu

(You then need small definitions of __global__, __shared__ and threadIdx yourself, since the CUDA headers are not included.)

The dependency-chain benchmark:

bench_ilp.c · c source

  // how much do independent accumulators matter?  float sum, no -ffast-math,
  // so the compiler must keep the order we wrote.
  #include <stdio.h>
  #include <time.h>
  #define N 4096
                          // 16 KB of floats: fits in the L1 cache
  #define REPS 200000
  static float a[N];
  static double now(void){ struct timespec t; clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC,&t); return t.tv_sec+t.tv_nsec*1e-9; }

  __attribute__((noinline)) float sum1(const float *x){
      float s = 0;
      for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) s += x[i];
                                                       // every add waits for the
  previous add
      return s;
  }
  __attribute__((noinline)) float sum4(const float *x){
      float s0=0, s1=0, s2=0, s3=0;
                                                       // 4 independent chains
      for (int i = 0; i < N; i += 4){ s0+=x[i]; s1+=x[i+1]; s2+=x[i+2]; s3+=x[i+3]; }return (s0+s1)+(s2+s3);
  }
  __attribute__((noinline)) float sum8(const float *x){
      float s0=0,s1=0,s2=0,s3=0,s4=0,s5=0,s6=0,s7=0;
                                                      // 8 independent chains
      for (int i = 0; i < N; i += 8){ s0+=x[i]; s1+=x[i+1]; s2+=x[i+2]; s3+=x[i+3];s4+=x[i+4]; s5+=x[i+5]; s6+=x[i+6];
  s7+=x[i+7]; }
      return ((s0+s1)+(s2+s3))+((s4+s5)+(s6+s7));
  }
  int main(void){
      for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) a[i] = (float)(i % 7) * 0.5f;
      float (*f[3])(const float*) = {sum1, sum4, sum8}; const char *name[3] = {"1
  chain ", "4 chains", "8 chains"};
      volatile float sink = 0;
      for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++){
          double t0 = now(); for (int r = 0; r < REPS; r++) sink += f[k](a); double t= now() - t0;
          printf("%s
                      %.3f ns per element\n", name[k], t * 1e9 / ((double)N * REPS));}
      return 0;
  }

  // pointer chasing: each load gives the address of the next load,
  // so the cpu cannot start load k+1 before load k finishes. this measures latency.#include <stdio.h>
  #include <stdlib.h>
  #include <time.h>
  static double now(void){ struct timespec t; clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC,&t); return t.tv_sec+t.tv_nsec*1e-9; }
  int main(void){
      size_t sizes_kb[] = {16, 64, 512, 2048, 16384, 131072, 524288};
      for (int s = 0; s < 7; s++){
          size_t n = sizes_kb[s] * 1024 /
  64;
                 // one node per 64-byte cache line
          char *mem = aligned_alloc(64, n * 64);
          size_t *order = malloc(n * sizeof *order);
          for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) order[i] = i;
          for (size_t i = n - 1; i > 0; i--){ size_t j = ((size_t)rand() * RAND_MAX +rand()) % (i + 1);
              size_t t = order[i]; order[i] = order[j]; order[j] = t; }
          for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++)
                                                          // random cycle through alllines
              *(char**)(mem + order[i] * 64) = mem + order[(i + 1) % n] * 64;
          char *p = mem + order[0] * 64;
          size_t steps = 20000000;
          for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) p = *(char**)p;
                                                          // warm up
          double t0 = now();
          for (size_t i = 0; i < steps; i++) p = *(char**)p;
          double t = now() - t0;
          printf("%8zu KB   %6.1f ns per load   %s\n", sizes_kb[s], t * 1e9 / steps,p ? "" : "x");
          free(mem); free(order);
      }
  }

  // the same loop over the same values, unsorted versus sorted.
  // the branch inside is unpredictable on random data and almost free on sorted data.#include <stdio.h>
  #include <stdlib.h>
  #include <time.h>
  #define N (1 << 20)
  static int a[N];
  static double now(void){ struct timespec t; clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC,&t); return t.tv_sec+t.tv_nsec*1e-9; }
  static int cmp(const void *x, const void *y){ return *(const int*)x - *(const
  int*)y; }
  __attribute__((noinline)) long sum_big(const int *x, long n){
      long s = 0;
      for (long i = 0; i < n; i++)
          if (x[i] >= 128) s += x[i];
                                           // taken about half the time
      return s;
  }
  int main(void){
      srand(1); for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) a[i] = rand() % 256;
      volatile long sink;
      for (int pass = 0; pass < 2; pass++){
          if (pass == 1) qsort(a, N, sizeof a[0], cmp);
          sink = sum_big(a, N);
          double t0 = now(); for (int r = 0; r < 50; r++) sink = sum_big(a, N);
  double t = now() - t0;
          printf("%s %.2f ns per element\n", pass ? "sorted:  " : "unsorted:", t *
  1e9 / (50.0 * N));
      }
      return 0;
  }
